title: Is the Hope at AFM Real?
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All November 10, 2026 8:55am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything Courtesy of A24 Film execs heading to L.A. for the American Film Market may be feeling something they haven’t in a while: hope. Disruption still reigns, but independent and specialty fare has had a run of breakouts at the North American box office, topped by this weekend’s launch of Godzilla Minus Zero . The sequel from GKIDS and Toho opened to an estimated $32 million, well above the distributor’s mid-$20 millions projection. Takashi Yamazaki’s follow-up to the Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One (2023) reportedly cost in the mid-teens and is being touted as the biggest live-action foreign-language opening since 2004’s Hero , which bowed with $17.8 million. Related Stories Movies Brandon Sklenar on 'Iron Jane,' Body Dysmorphia and His Rapid Hollywood Rise Movies Claes Bang, Valerie Pachner Drama 'I Is Another' Sells Wide Ahead of AFM It isn’t the only surprise. A24’s You Can See Everything , the Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, is entering blockbuster territory, having grossed almost $80 million domestically. That’s a rare result for nonfiction in a theatrical market that has been unkind to documentaries, and the film is only beginning to roll out internationally. Niche programming is delivering, too. Angel Studios’ faith-based Drummer Boy , from directors Ben and Joel David Smallbone, opened to around $9 million. Nitesh Tiwari’s Indian epic Ramayana: Rise of a Legend , handled in the U.S. by Sony, grossed an estimated $8.6 million in its first weekend, on the widest domestic launch ever for an Indian film. Add this year’s indie horror run, from Obsession ($500 million worldwide and counting) to Backrooms ($400 million-plus) and the self-distributed Iron Lung ($50 million-plus), and the makings of a good-vibes AFM are in place. For sellers, the biggest takeaway is that audiences are showing up, and that they are young. Sarah Lebutsch, head of sales at U.K. group Protagonist Pictures, points to You Can See Everything as proof that a smart campaign and the right timing can still produce a hit. “Look at what You Can See Everything is doing at the moment in the U.S. It’s incredible,” she says. She is equally encouraged by who is buying tickets. “It’s great to see those sorts of box office results, and the fact that Gen Z are going, and Gen Alpha are going and seeing films together in cinemas,” Lebutsch says. “There is a big resurgence of that, which I think we should all be very, very encouraged by.” Policy may help, too. California Gov. Gavin Newsom is pushing a major expansion of the state’s film and TV tax credit program, proposing to raise the annual credit from $750 million to $1 billion. The incentive has been crucial for keeping projects in the state. Newsom is also backing the bipartisan effort in Congress, championed by President Trump, to create a national film and TV tax incentive that would stack with each state’s own credits. For indie producers piecing together financing, having a federal layer on top of state incentives would be a significant and much-needed change. The presale market, long AFM’s foundation, also appears to be holding up. “At Protagonist, we’ve always done very well out of the AFM,” Lebutsch says. “Presales have always worked really well for us there. The big buyers from across the world, they’ll all be there to pick up packages.” Protagonist will be shopping It’s All Right , with Paul Bettany as an aging rock star and Asha Banks as a rising singer who, unbeknownst to her, is his forgotten daughter from a one-night stand. The online creator-to-director pipeline will be a major talking point at this year’s AFM. Seemingly all the hot young horror directors honed their craft, and built their respective fan bases, online before their theatrical breakouts. “The film industry can certainly learn from creators that storytelling doesn’t need to be limited necessarily to strict forms,” says veteran horror producer Steven Schneider ( Paranormal Activity , Insidious ), whose Spooky Pictures recently scored a hit with Hokum , which has grossed $25 million worldwide on a $5 million budget. “Stories can begin online, narratives can be told, shared and expanded through shortform videos and parsed out over time in a way that builds awareness and excitement. Creators have shown incredible prowess in meeting their audiences where they’re at.” But Schneider cautions that success online does not always translate to cinemas. “Traditional storytelling conventions and techniques are established for good reason,” he says. “We want to innovate and bridge the gap between an online audience and a theatrical one, but it’s important to respect the differences in the form.” Traditional filmmaking, he argues, can “connect more deeply and profoundly with an audience through intricate storytelling,” and that craft “shouldn’t be dismissed in favor of virality or easy dopamine hits.” Not every indie package at AFM will become the next Obsession or You Can See Everything . But audiences are returning, U.S. tax incentives are on the horizon and a new generation of filmmakers is packing theaters with younger fans. For a market that for years felt like it was in terminal decline, that’s reason enough to cheer. THR

title: BMG’s Concord Originals Preps Supernatural Gothic Horror Pic ‘Wolf at the Door’ (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: × Nov 10, 2026 8:45am PT BMG’s Concord Originals Preps Supernatural Gothic Horror Pic ‘Wolf at the Door’ (EXCLUSIVE) The five-year-old division is taking a 360-degree approach to an expanded portfolio following Concord's merger with music and theater powerhouse BMG and acquisition of RKO's classic film library By Anna Marie de la Fuente Plus Icon Anna Marie de la Fuente @adelafuente1 Latest Disney+ and ‘The House of Flowers’ Director Manolo Caro Prep Series Adaptation of ‘Blood Wedding’ by Federico García Lorca (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago ‘Longlegs’ Star Alicia Witt Toplines Colombian Horror Thriller ‘Incuba Project,’ Directed by Chile’s Juan Pablo Arias (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago ‘The Cry of Serankwa,’ an Indigenous Eco-Thriller and Triple Sanfic Industria Award Winner, Strikes Distribution Deal for Latin America 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Sophia Dilley, Charles Hopkins Courtesy of Concord Originals The full moon is out at Concord Originals , the film and TV arm of music and theater powerhouse BMG , where it is developing and producing supernatural gothic horror feature “Wolf at the Door.” Based on the eponymous play from Concord Theatricals, the genre pic will be helmed by Argentina’s Agustina San Martín, who recently directed the psychological horror feature “Psyche,” starring Noah Jupe (“A Quiet Place”) and Isabela Merced (“The Last of Us”), currently in post. Related Stories Raye to Headline BST Hyde Park With Sienna Spiro Opening Raye Named Variety’s 2026 Hitmaker of the Year The adaptation is written by playwright, poet and screenwriter Marisela Treviño Orta, based on her play “Wolf at the Door,” part of a trilogy of theatrical productions inspired by Latinx mythology and the Brothers Grimm fairy tales. ‘Wolf at the Door’ Credit: Liz Lauren Set in 19th century New Mexico, it centers on a young woman, close to giving birth to her first child, who foretells the return of a malevolent half-man half-wolf creature, only to discover that another predator has already entrenched itself in her hacienda. Casting is underway. “Wolf at the Door” is produced by Concord Originals’ Emmy-nominated exec VP Sophia Dilley (HBO’s “Stax: Soulsville, USA”) and VP of development Charles Hopkins (“Billy Preston: That’s the Way God Planned It”). Concord Originals’ Quíle Miguel Gomez, Victor Zaraya and Bob Valentine executive produce. “We’re film executives within a music and theater company, and this is the first play we’ve commissioned and developed entirely in-house. I’m really excited about what this represents and how it demonstrates our team’s ability to go beyond simply packaging and building projects,” said Dilley. Hopkins concurred: “This project encapsulates exactly what Concord Originals is all about: identifying world-class IP under the BMG roof and reimagining it for screen.” The eight-person team of this r elatively young division, founded in 2021, has its work cut out for it, given the deep vaults of BMG’s catalog plus those of Concord Theatricals (18,000+) and the recent acquisition of RKO, which adds another 5,000+ IP assets, including such classic cinema titles as Alfred Hitchcock’s “Suspicion” and Fritz Lang’s “The Woman in the Window.” “RKO has such a rich history and so much of it hasn’t been oversaturated, which makes it ripe for reinvention and a chance to reach new generations. It also feels like a deep well of stories that’s particularly timely for where the industry is today. Historically, RKO was interesting in how it made films on contained budgets, and I’m excited to explore what that approach could look like today,” Dilley remarked. Concord Originals’ scripted slate also includes “Bleeding Love,” an original movie musical featuring hits from multi Grammy-winner Ryan Tedder, a limited series adaptation of Rodgers & Hammerstein’s “Cinderella” with Skydance TV and projects with Jennifer Lopez ’s Nuyorican Prods. for Disney+. Reflecting on the fact that “Wolf” director San Martin is a protégé of BMG client Lin-Manuel Miranda for the Rolex Mentor and Protégé Arts Initiative, Hopkins said: “That is the advantage we now have in this bigger organization, is that there are these connecting dots between all of the talent that we work with on the filmmaking side as well as the music and theater side. So I think we’ll encounter more and more of those common connections among the artists we work with in the future.” Dilley pointed out that a single property could generate a film, stage production, album and other associated content. “We cover so many different areas, so the exciting part is bringing them together. Our ambition is to take a 360 approach to projects wherever we can, connecting film and TV with music and theater … bringing artists into a series, playwrights into the writing process, or developing a film that also has a stage production and an accompanying album,” said Dilley. “We have the opportunity to be involved in the life cycle of these copyrights, from beginning to end. Ultimately, it’s about keeping artists, iconic legacies and great IP in the zeitgeist, championing them and giving them the biggest cultural impact possible. title: Millie Bobby Brown To Star In, Produce Netflix Comedy ‘Non-Refundable’; Jack Innanen Also Set
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Matt Grobar Matt Grobar Senior Film Reporter More Stories By Matt ‘Being Heumann’ Composer Francesco Le Metre Tapped Into Judy Heumann’s Drive And A ’70s Punk Rock Spirit – Sound & Screen Film Alaskan Crime Procedural ‘Wild Life’ From Juliet Lashinsky-Revene In Development At NBC Untitled Signs Nnamdi Asomugha & His iAm21 Entertainment Banner View All November 10, 2026 8:45am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Millie Bobby Brown and Jack Innanen Michael Schwartz/Jack Innanen EXCLUSIVE: After wrapping up Stranger Things and capping off an Enola Holmes trilogy, and with a David Harbour co-starring spy comedy upcoming, Millie Bobby Brown has found her next project with Netflix : a comedy titled Non-Refundable that she’ll produce and headline opposite Jack Innanen , the breakout star of FX’s Adults . With Emmy-nominated SNL alum Paul Briganti aboard to direct, Non-Refundable is billed as a high-concept commercial comedy centered on Nate (Innanen) and Dani (Brown), an ex-couple who are still on the hook for their wedding venue despite breaking up. This leads them to travel to Mexico out of spite, where they try showing each other up with new dates. Related Stories News 'The Perfect Lie' Actor Matthijs Van De Sande Bakhuyzen To Lead AFM-Bound Arctic Thriller 'The Art Of Survival' News 'Swapped' Composer Siddhartha Khosla Used Music From Every Continent For Netflix's Animated Adventure - Sound & Screen Film Pic is based on a spec by David Bernstein. Bobby Brown and Jake Bongiovi will produce for PCMA ( Damsel , Enola Holmes ), alongside Andrew Swett and Aaron Ryder for Embrace Entertainment (Netflix’s Office Romance ) and Will Speck and Josh Gordon for Speck + Gordon Inc. Executive producers are Bobby Brown for PCMA, Eric Fineman and David Kern. Watch on Deadline Sources said Non-Refundable reflects Netflix’s interest in revitalizing a version of the rom-com you see less of these days — a film like Forgetting Sarah Marshall that had big laughs and emotional stakes in equal measure. Execs were on the lookout for fresh takes and knew they’d found the one in new writer Bernstein’s spec when the team started quoting its one-liners and referencing its set pieces around the office. At Netflix, Brown has become synonymous with megahit genre fare like Stranger Things , Damsel and the Enola Holmes films. But execs thought of her after seeing her performance in Just Picture It , an upcoming Netflix rom-com where she stars opposite The Fabelmans’ Gabriel LaBelle, which speaks to underappreciated comedic chops. Innanen wowed Netflix execs with his turn as Paul Baker in Adults , an FX hang-out sitcom compared to a Gen Z version of Friends or New Girl . Meanwhile, Briganti was the choice to direct given his work at SNL spanning six seasons, where he demonstrated an eye for surprising, off-the-wall humor, as well as a knack for getting the best out of talent. During his time there as segment director across Digital Shorts and more, select highlights included working on breakout Please Don’t Destroy videos, including “Three Sad Virgins” (feat. Taylor Swift), and directing Brad Pitt to an Emmy nomination via a Covid-era cold open segment where he played Dr. Anthony Fauci. Wrapping up her five seasons with Stranger Things on New Year’s Eve 2025, Bobby Brown is fresh off Enola Holmes 3 , which nabbed over 20M views in its first five days alone. Upcoming, she’s set to reunite with her Stranger Things dad David Harbour on a father-daughter espionage thriller for Netflix from Adolescence ‘s Jack Thorne & A24. She is repped by WME and Hansen, Jacobson. Seen over the summer in the second season of the critically acclaimed Adults — which seemed to have broadened awareness around the series — Innanen has also previously been seen starring opposite Dan Levy in Netflix’s crime comedy Big Mistakes from Levy and Rachel Sennott. The Canadian actor is repped by UTA, Range Media Partners and Sloane, Offer, Weber & Dern. Briganti reteamed with Please Don’t Destroy post-SNL on the Peacock comedy Please Don’t Destroy: The Legend of Foggy Mountain . He previously intersected with Innanen as the director of multiple episodes of Adults and began his career making videos for CollegeHumor, where he went on to become site director. He garnered early attention for the Hugo Award-nominated satirical video “Fuck Me, Ray Bradbury,” starring Crazy Ex-Girlfriend’s Rachel Bloom, before going on to work on series including The Late Late Show with James Corden , Adam Ruins Everything , Crazy Ex-Girlfriend , Chad and At Home with Amy Sedaris , to name a few. He is repped by WME, Mosaic and Ginsburg Daniels. Speck and Gordon, the filmmakers behind Blades of Glory and Office Christmas Party , are repped by 3 Arts and CAA. title: As Russell Brand’s Begins a 10-Year Prison Sentence, Why Celebrities Fear the Power of an Expose
full_text: × Nov 10, 2026 8:42am PT As Russell Brand’s Begins a 10-Year Prison Sentence, Why Celebrities Fear the Power of an Expose By K.J. Yossman Plus Icon K.J. Yossman @KJYossman Latest As Russell Brand’s Begins a 10-Year Prison Sentence, Why Celebrities Fear the Power of an Expose 13 minutes ago David Walliams Dropped by Agency Following ‘Grooming’ Allegations 34 minutes ago David Walliams, Former ‘Britain’s Got Talent’ Judge, Accused of ‘Grooming Fans’ as Young as 15 After Failing to Get Injunction 4 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source LEON NEAL Standing in the glass dock at Southwark Crown Court in London, awaiting his sentence for one rape and three sexual assaults to be handed down, Russell Brand was addressed directly by the judge. “No doubt your companions thought it was outrageous laddish behaviour that only you could get away with,” Justice Bennathan said, referencing an incident in which Brand had launched himself on an unknown woman in the middle of a studio corridor as his entourage looked on. “It was outrageous and possibly laddish, but also a criminal sexual offence. And as it turns out, you haven’t got away with it.” Related Stories Olivia Rodrigo, Katseye and Sienna Spiro to Be Honored at Variety’s 10th Annual Hitmakers Event Raye to Headline BST Hyde Park With Sienna Spiro Opening Brand may well have gotten away with it had it not been for a joint investigation by Channel 4 documentary strand “Dispatches” and The Sunday Times of London. Their reporting, published in Sept. 2023, contained numerous serious allegations, including that the former comedian had sexually assaulted four women between 2006 and 2013. Brand denied any wrongdoing (none of the women who made the allegations in the documentary were involved in the recent criminal trial although it is understood the Met Police are now investigating at least one of those complaints and Brand may face yet more charges). The former comedian, who’d appeared in Hollywood movies and had a short-lived marriage to Katy Perry at the height of her success, had long cultivated an air of degeneracy as part of his persona, enabling him to operate in plain sight. Yet it wasn’t until the Channel 4/Sunday Times investigation was published that police opened an investigation. Whether it’s because the reporting had prompted more women to come forward – as Brand’s lawyer in the trial, Ian Winter, repeatedly argued — or because the media spotlight gave the authorities the resolution they needed to investigate a celebrity will probably never be known. But Brand is not the only celebrity to have found themselves in the dock after being accused of wrongdoing in the media. In 2023 news anchor Huw Edwards , once the best-known and highest paid journalist at the BBC, was the subject of an expose by The Sun, who revealed he had been in an inappropriate text-based relationship with a teenager during which he’d paid for nude photographs. Although he had not acted unlawfully in that instance, Edwards was arrested less than a year later and eventually convicted of making indecent images after police found videos of children as young as seven being abused on Edwards’ phone. It emerged he had been sent them by a pedophile to whom he’d, apparently unrelatedly, gifted numerous instalments of cash. Kevin Spacey has also faced an endless series of legal battles – both criminal and civil on both sides of the Atlantic – after he was accused of sexually assaulting a 14-year-old boy in a 2017 Buzzfeed interview. None have resulted in any finding of liability or criminality and Spacey has always denied any allegations of sexual misconduct but his career has never recovered. In the U.K. Spacey was, like Brand, tried at Southwark Crown Court, where he was on trial for nine charges of sexual assault against four separate men. He was acquitted on all counts . After the trial, some of the jurors asked to meet the Oscar-winner and shake his hand. So it’s unsurprising that David Walliams, a comedian, bestselling children’s author and former “Britain’s Got Talent” judge, sought an injunction last month to prevent the same newspaper from publishing an investigation into his alleged sexual misconduct. Lawyers for Walliams told London’s High Court he would be likely to commit suicide if the story was published. The judge held that suicidal ideation is not a ground on which to prevent the publication of an article potentially in the public interest, although he noted his decision to dismiss the injunction does not mean the allegations are true. Published today, the Guardian’s report accuses Walliams of grooming young fans and harassment. One woman told the newspaper she was 15 when she alleges Walliams drove her to his house and engaged in behavior that she now considers to be sexual assault. Walliams has denied all the allegations. There is no police investigation into Walliams nor any suggestion he may face charges, but, like Spacey, his career now lies in ruins. (Walliams has been dropped by his agent and his books will no longer be published). Brand’s celebrity loomed large throughout his trial: some of his victims were fans who were initially thrilled to meet him, others were vulnerable because of his disproportionate power over them. In his sentencing remarks, Justice Bennathan accepted the former comedian’s fame was “an intrinsic part of each offence” as it allowed him to carry out his crimes. But, he noted, “I also need to be careful I am not punishing you more because you are famous.” Coddled by their managers, obeyed by their assistants and adored by their fans, some celebrities have been able to abuse their exalted status. title: Jordan Fisher to Star as the Kid in Broadway’s ‘Purple Rain’
full_text: × Nov 10, 2026 8:37am PT Jordan Fisher to Star as the Kid in Broadway’s ‘Purple Rain’ By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest Jordan Fisher to Star as the Kid in Broadway’s ‘Purple Rain’ 11 minutes ago David Ellison on DC Shakeup: Jeremy Latcham Will ‘Build the Future of DC,’ Praises James Gunn and Peter Safran’s ‘Passion’ 22 hours ago Box Office: ‘Heated Rivalry’ Fans Drive Show’s Theatrical Release to $1.4 Million 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jordan Fisher will portray “The Kid,” the iconic role made famous by Prince, in Broadway ‘s “ Purple Rain .” Fisher is a theater veteran, having appeared in musicals like “Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street,” “Moulin Rouge! The Musical,” “Dear Evan Hansen” and “Hamilton,” but this marks the first time he’s originating a role on Broadway. “We know that Jordan Fisher is an extraordinary talent, but what’s been thrilling about watching him inhabit ‘The Kid’ is discovering the fire beneath the surface: the swagger, vulnerability and restless creative spirit we recognize in Prince,” said director Saheem Ali. “Jordan brings all of that to the role, along with an infectious generosity that makes everyone around him better. He’s finding something raw, surprising, and deeply human in this iconic character, and I can’t wait for Broadway audiences to experience it.” Related Stories Raye to Headline BST Hyde Park With Sienna Spiro Opening Raye Wins Mercury Prize for Album of the Year An alternate performer will play the role of “The Kid” on Tuesday evenings and Wednesday matinees. Additional casting will be announced at a later date. “Purple Rain” will premiere next spring at the Majestic Theatre, with previews beginning on March 12 ahead of opening night on April 12. The show is based on the 1984 classic, which became a box office hit with nearly $100 million worldwide and inspired the mega-selling album of the same name. Here’s the show’s official logline: “Minneapolis, 1984. A new era of music television is creating overnight stars. A magnetic young performer known as ‘The Kid’ seems like the perfect frontman to lead his bandmates to stardom. But when his past threatens everything he’s built, he’ll have to sing his way out of the darkness and into the spotlight where he belongs.” The stage adaptation features over 20 of Prince’s iconic hits, including “When Doves Cry,” “I Would Die 4 U,” “Take Me With You” and “The Beautiful Ones.” Peter Duchan (“Dogfight”) wrote the musical’s book, while Jason Michael Webb (“MJ the Musical) is leading the music team. Bobby Z and Morris Hayes, both of whom worked with Prince for years as bandmates and musical collaborators, serve the production as music advisers. The musical was first staged in 2025 at Hennepin Theatre Trust’s historic State Theatre in Minneapolis, where Prince was born. title: Josh Van Valkenburg Named President of Universal Publishing Nashville, Troy Tomlinson Moves to Exclusive Advisor
full_text: × Nov 10, 2026 8:36am PT Josh Van Valkenburg Named President of Universal Publishing Nashville, Troy Tomlinson Moves to Exclusive Advisor By Jem Aswad Plus Icon Jem Aswad Executive Editor, Music jemaswad Latest Raye Named Variety’s 2026 Hitmaker of the Year 37 minutes ago Kanye West Breaks His Own Record for Biggest Rap Concert in U.S. History — Again — With 83,132 Fans 24 hours ago Richard Lloyd, Television’s Fiery and Fluent Guitarist, Dies at 75 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Josh Van Valkenburg has been named president of Universal Music Publishing Group Nashville, it was announced by UMPG chairman & CEO Jody Gerson. Van Valkenburg will report to Gerson, be based in Nashville and assume his position on January 4, 2027, as longtime UMPG Nashville chairman & CEO Troy Tomlinson transitions to an exclusive advisory role, according to the announcement. Related Stories Raye Wins Mercury Prize for Album of the Year Raye to Headline BST Hyde Park With Sienna Spiro Opening In his new position, Van Valkenburg will oversee the management and creative direction of UMPG Nashville, leading the team in identifying, signing and developing emerging talent and supporting its acclaimed roster of songwriters, artists and producers. Van Valkenburg was most recently executive VP of creative at Sony Music Publishing Nashville, promoted to that role in 2021 after joining the company in 2015. Over the years he has worked closely with such talents as ASCAP Songwriter of the Year Josh Osborne, four-time BMI Songwriter of the Year Ross Copperman and SESAC Songwriter of the Year Jon Nite. He launched his music publishing career at EMI in 2006. In making the announcement, Gerson said, “Country music is more global today than at any time in its history, and the opportunities for Nashville’s songwriters have never been greater. Josh brings the vision, ambition and leadership skills to build on that momentum, along with deep relationships throughout the creative community and a gift for identifying and developing exceptional songwriters. I’m thrilled to welcome him to UMPG and look forward to all he and our Nashville team will accomplish together.” Van Valkenburg added, “Jody Gerson is an exceptional leader who remains steadfastly passionate about fighting for creatives and their art. I’m grateful for her trust and the opportunity to lead UMPG Nashville into its next chapter. I want to honor Troy Tomlinson for his genuine love of songwriters, his willingness to share his wisdom and experience with the many of us who look up to him, and his long-standing leadership within UMPG and the greater Nashville creative community.” Tomlinson has served as chairman and CEO of UMPG Nashville since 2019. Over more than four decades, he has worked closely with such artists as Taylor Swift, Kenny Chesney, Megan Moroney, Keith Urban, Luke Bryan, Brooks & Dunn and Kelsea Ballerini; and writers including Chase McGill, Tom Douglas, Tony Lane, Jim Beavers, Rodney Crowell, Dean Dillon and Casey Beathard. He previously served as President and CEO of Sony/ATV Nashville from 2005 to 2019, having joined the company in 2002. Before Sony/ATV, he spent 15 years at Acuff-Rose Music Publishing. He previously led the Nashville division of Fame Music Publishing. title: R.J. Mitte’s Final Director Dedicates Film to Late Actor: “I Can’t Believe He’s Not Here to See It”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Jeffrey Levine, as Told to Jackie Strause Plus Icon Jeffrey Levine, as Told to Jackie Strause View All November 10, 2026 8:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source RJ Mitte at a screening of 'Talking To Strangers' on Sept. 30 in Beverly Hills, California. Unique Nicole/Getty Images Jeffrey Levine is executive producer of Morph Media , and producer/writer/director on R.J. Mitte ’s final movie, SNAFU: Situation Normal All F’d Up (working title). *** This is the beginning of a beautiful friendship. That was how I felt the last time I saw R.J. Mitte. Several weeks before his death, I drove R.J. to the airport. We had just finished filming for our movie that R.J. was featured in. R.J. was leaving Los Angeles and was heading back home for a quick turnaround to London for a convention. Related Stories Movies Giancarlo Esposito and John Turturro Hated Each Other on 'Do the Right Thing.' Now They Break Character to Cry Mid-Scene News R.J. Mitte's Mother Shares Tribute After His Death: "We Are Lost Without Him" The ride took about two hours, and when we arrived at LAX, I got out of the car and I hugged him. I said, “I’ll see you soon.” And he said what he always said, “Let me know if you need anything.” That’s just who R.J. was. My experience with R.J. was over a shorter period of time than many of the people who have been speaking out since his unexpected death. There are a lot of people who knew R.J. better than me. But he was the type of person where it didn’t matter how long or how short you knew him. Once you did, you knew the real him. He wasn’t an actor who just did a scene and left. He was bigger than that, a positive force, and we were just starting our friendship. I first met R.J. in May of this year, when our executive producer, Bradford Rand, cast him in our movie, SNAFU: Situation Normal All F’d Up (working title). We had our first conversation over Zoom, the three of us, about him playing an AI executive in our social impact film. It began as a smaller part. And from the second Bradford put me on the phone with R.J. and he heard that our mission for the film was to impact the lives of kids, he said, “I’m in.” That was my experience with him from that day on. We would talk about the character and the story, because R.J. really cared about this movie, and his role evolved as we produced the film. It became very important for me to have an impactful character arc for him. In the story — after criminals exploit the protagonist’s teenage son — R.J.’s character, an AI developer, is asked to help, and he begins to reflect on the far-reaching negative impact of AI. R.J.’s character uses his position for good and, in the end, he faces a pivotal decision on whether or not to walk away from his high-paying executive job to create what I am hoping someone with influence will one day execute: a global AI regulation company. R.J. Mitte and Jeffrey Lewis on set. Courtesy The film will inform parents about the dangers of social media and AI, but in a commercial and entertaining way. The objective is for parents to be able to start a dialogue with their kids about the far-reaching effects of AI, social media and our changing media landscape. And it’s R.J.’s character who says, “Enough. We have to do something.” It’s such an impactful character, and I just can’t believe he’s not here today to see it. Our independent film deals with mental health, which isn’t lost on me now. We wrapped filming not too long ago. We’re currently in post-production. We are in talks on distribution and hope to get the film in front of as many people as possible. But as I’m watching assemblies now, it’s emotionally wrenching. And then there’s R.J.’s extensive behind-the-scenes video addressing AI, and I can’t bring myself to watch that right now. R.J.’s scenes were so good. It’s crazy how his authenticity carries on screen through the character. Pure talent. Being a part of our project, for R.J., was always about the impact. It was never about money or fame. He wanted the character to be as true, real and impactful as he could be. And he delivered in spades. This film is the first in a slate for our social impact feature division. I couldn’t imagine a better person to carry this torch. I find myself thinking about R.J. and all the things we talked about, and all the things he truly cared about — his mom and his sister and his fiancé and his work with the Mitte Foundation . R.J. was pure good. It’s a level of human being you don’t see very often. During our two-hour drive to the airport, he spoke about his foundation and what he wanted to do. He truly wanted to make a difference. He felt like he had a deeper purpose. I asked, “How can we help?” And we talked details, and I’m confident that we will. We’ve been working with the Sentinel Foundation, which deals with the exploitation of kids, and its Clinical Director, Dr. Ashley Poklar, who flew out to be on set during filming. The end of our movie will include a QR code that will direct viewers to resources, both for parents to be able to talk to their children, and for teens who may be going through something and need to know where to go for help. When I would finish directing a scene with R.J., he’d say, “Are you happy, Jeff? Because if you’re happy, I’m happy.” I am so sad that he suffered and that this happened. What we can do for R.J. now is to keep our promise. Honor what we set out to do, and why he signed up to make our film in the first place. Create awareness, dialogue and impact as many people as we can. Our film is dedicated to R.J., and for anybody who is going through something. We want our message to reach anyone who needs to hear it. You are never alone. I didn’t know R.J. for a very long time. But the time I knew him, I’ll never forget. THR

title: Jacob Elordi To Star In Adaptation Of ‘The Executioner’s Song’ From United Artists
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Justin Kroll Justin Kroll Film Editor @krolljvar More Stories By Justin Aaron And Adam Nee Board Live-Action ‘Catan’ Movie At Netflix Departing DC Co-Head James Gunn Reflects On “Trying” Four Years, Juggling Being Filmmaker & Exec WME Sets Expanded Leadership Group View All November 10, 2026 8:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jacob Elordi; 'The Executioner's Song' Getty Images EXCLUSIVE: Scott Stuber’s United Artists has acquired the rights to the 1982 motion picture The Executioner’s Song and set Oscar nominee Jacob Elordi to star. title: AI Takes Center Stage at Tech-Forward AFM With Innovation Hub and AFM House Expansion
full_text: × Nov 10, 2026 8:23am PT AI Takes Center Stage at Tech-Forward AFM With Innovation Hub and AFM House Expansion By Corbin Bolies Plus Icon Corbin Bolies Latest Elvis Music Owners, Eminem Publisher File Sprawling New Lawsuits Against AI Music Generator Suno: ‘The Next Elvis Won’t Pick Up a Guitar’ 3 days ago Netflix Names Mattel Executive Roberto Stanichi as VP of Consumer Products and Experiences 5 days ago How Grimes’ Cameo in Theater-Bound AI Film ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Came Together (EXCLUSIVE) 5 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy IFTA First it came for the films, then the film festivals. Now, AI has taken hold of this year’s American Film Market. The five-day independent film marketplace in Los Angeles, produced by the Independent Film and Television Alliance, already has a splashy year planned, with pic packages on offer, including a new Armando Iannucci film and A24’s expensive “Elden Ring” adaptation. But as producers and distributors go about buying and selling movies, they’ll do so as the film industry’s third rail — artificial intelligence — takes center stage. The 2026 edition will see the market’s Innovation Hub, a space where exhibitors showcase new technologies gripping Hollywood, expand into its inaugural “ AFM House,” a 15,000-square-foot space across from the AFM HQ at the Fairmont Century Plaza. The list of companies participating has also expanded, with nearly 20 firms eager to highlight their own technology and a suite of new panels discussing AI’s impact. The Hub launched last year in collaboration with the Marché du Film, the Cannes Film Festival’s cinema marketplace that proved to be very AI-friendly this year. But this year’s extensive expansion of the Hub, and the prominence of AI, represents the latest example of Hollywood’s growing tolerance for the technology in how films are produced, sold and distributed — all tenets of AFM. “Technology is going to be a key driver, no matter where you sit on kind of AI,” says Jackie Brenneman, who is shepherding her first AFM after taking the reins as IFTA president in January. “AI as a creative tool — there’s a lot more debate on that than AI as a really great way to analyze data and make predictions. That’s what AI has been doing for a long time, and so AI serves lots of different roles. At AFM, we’re not here to make a judgment call, but I do think that a lot of the tools … are much more in the latter [category], in using AI and data to help people make better decisions or do things better, faster, cheaper, and less on just AI as the next full-scale studio. But of course, we have room for all.” Such an expansion in space for the Innovation Hub means an expansion of the companies set to populate it. Returning to AFM is Largo.ai, a Sylvester Stallone-backed Swiss firm that uses AI to help brands, studios and creatives determine whether their idea is producible. The company was founded in 2018 as an offshoot of the Swiss university EPFL, back when AI was simply “machine learning” and the AI agents we’ve come to know and somewhat fear were merely the product of science fiction. Its collection of tools includes simulated focus groups and projections to see which actors could best fit a character, providing independent filmmakers with the tools usually reserved for the deep-pocketed Hollywood studios. Largo’s chief panel at AFM includes a “Shark Tank”-style pitch presentation, where producers working with the firm will showcase for distributors and financiers how Largo’s platform can help analyze the commercial viability of their projects. Sami Arpa, the firm’s CEO, says Largo is mindful of fears that film production can be too data-driven and argues the company is more “data-assisted” than eager to infuse AI into the creative process. “In the tools specifically, we never tell people what to do,” he says. “There are tools a bit going beyond that,” he admits. “They are replacing full human creativity. Obviously, people are feeling danger from that, and I think they have the right to feel that danger. But with our experience, we don’t think the audience is welcoming full AI-generated content if a human still is not at the center of the creativity.” For those in Hollywood who do want to create fully AI-generated content, enter Oxen.ai. The company, founded in 2022 by IBM veteran Greg Schoeninger, works as both a platform for creators to build AI shots with a selection of AI models and as a studio to produce AI shots for vendors. Some of the creatives who’ve used its tools come from Disney, Google and Live Nation. The platform differentiates itself from other similar all-in-one model aggregators such as Higgsfield and OpenArt by publicly outlining the token cost for each model it offers before anyone pays a cent, including the pennies it costs to use Black Forest Labs’ FLUX models and the $55-per-million tokens Claude’s Fable model requires. It adds a layer of transparency to the use of AI that’s often obscured by monthly subscription costs offered by competing platforms, a fact Schoeninger takes great pride in. “It’s a subtle thing, but it’s a huge reason people switch,” he says. Schoeninger says AFM approached the company about appearing in the new AFM House after the startup’s “Cmd+Shift+Create” summit in September. At that event, professionals across the AI and creative landscape met and showcased how they’re weaving the technology into their work. He says the market’s expanded embrace of the technology reflects the “tipping point” the industry has reached, one where more Hollywood luminaries and executives are willing to go public about how they’re using AI despite the fear expressed by some of their peers over its impact on human jobs and creativity. “‘Jurassic Park’ is one of the first movies to do full visual effects,” he says, noting the few minutes in the 1993 film that contained computer-generated imagery. “It just felt like there was way more because of how Steven Spielberg used it in the film. I feel like we’re kind of in that era right now where, yeah, you might get ripped on if you’re doing a whole film in AI, but if you just use it for those shots that you need it, it seamlessly fades into the background or helps bring the film to life.” AI is also a focal point of some of AFM’s panels, such as the Producers Guild of America’s panel on “the AI Decisions Facing Film and TV Leaders” on the market’s main stage. The Cine Group, a Paris-based company that works with cinema operators, is bringing its Marché du Film-backed Cinemas Club to the AFM House and hosting a panel on how non-generative AI in the industry is a “utility rather than Tilly” — as in Norwood, the AI actress rankling Hollywood’s creatives. Patrick von Sychowski, the Cine Group’s international editor-in-chief and moderator of the panel, says the discussion is meant to reflect how AI already has a stronghold across film, and “sticking your head in the sand is not a solution.” AFM is representative of that ethos in its willingness to showcase the technology, he adds. “AFM under IFTA is not just moving with the times, but trying to stay a step or two ahead of the times in terms of what is required at these kinds of get-togethers,” von Sychowski says. “It’s such a unique opportunity to get together in person and bring together the right people for discussions, for deals, everything.” Being so public about embracing the technology does harbor some risk. Take the case of Urbanworld, the BIPOC-focused film festival that lost a yearslong sponsor in the AI-averse Writers Guild of America over its decision to host an AI program for its 30th edition last month. Big A-list festivals, such as Cannes, exclude AI-generated films from their official lineups. But Brenneman, while sensitive to people’s fears over the technology, says the purpose of the marketplace is to allow producers and financiers to determine what types of films emerge for public consumption. If they decide it’s AI films, then so be it. “We’re not a festival,” she says. “We are not making selections. We do not make judgment calls. That’s for the buyers. You know, the buyers are the ones who get to decide who it is that they want to support, what art it is that they think is commercial. title: Don’t Have 210 Spare GBs? ‘GTA VI’ Is Coming to Xbox Cloud Gaming (and the Xbox One) at Launch
full_text: × Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All November 10, 2026 8:19am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Grand Theft Auto VI Rockstar Games Grand Theft Auto VI is coming to Xbox Cloud Gaming at launch (Nov. 19), and will be playable on both the current-generation consoles (Xbox Series X|S) and the prior one (Xbox One). You read that right: Xbox One . Xbox said on Tuesday that GTA VI is “the most pre-ordered title of all time on the Microsoft Store.” The console-maker “encourage(s) everyone to begin pre-loading as soon as possible to ensure you’re prepared for launch day.” GTA VI is so massive (210 gbs) that it will take at least 10 hours to download. Many players will have to delete a number of other games from their library just to fit Grand Theft Auto VI . (You don’t lose ownership of the game, but you just have to re-install it to play again.) Or… don’t use a console at all! Grand Theft Auto VI will be playable on day one via Cloud Gaming at 1 a.m. ET. The game uses Xbox Series S graphics settings when cloud-streamed. (So actually downloading the game will still present the best-looking option for those with an Xbox Series X.) To cloud play, which allows for play away from your primary console, one still must purchase the game. PlayStation players do not (currently) have the cloud-play option, though the PlayStation 5 Pro still provides the single-best GTA VI playing experience possible. Win some, lose some. Here is a handy, Xbox-provided guide to how and when you can play Grand Theft Auto VI on or through its consoles: XBOX Series X: Play natively with the best XBOX console experience, available now to pre-install. XBOX Series S: The most affordable way to play GTA VI natively on XBOX, available now to pre-install. XBOX One: Stream Grand Theft Auto VI through XBOX Cloud Gaming on the XBOX One. You’ll need one of those three devices — smart TVs, browsers and devices like Amazon Fire sticks won’t cut it (for now). Other Rockstar Games like Grand Theft Auto V and Red Dead Redemption 2 are coming to Xbox Cloud Gaming “in the coming months,” Xbox said. Additionally, starting Wednesday, players in 29 supported markets can “buy cloud playtime to stream supported games without a Game Pass subscription,” per Xbox. (For 10 hours: $3.99, for 25 hours: $7.99, for 50 hours: $11.99.) THR

title: AFM 2026: Indie Film Faces a Tougher Market — But Theatrical Breakouts Offer Hope
full_text: × Nov 10, 2026 8:15am PT AFM 2026: Indie Film Faces a Tougher Market — But Theatrical Breakouts Offer Hope By Elsa Keslassy Plus Icon Elsa Keslassy International Correspondent @elsakeslassy Latest AFM 2026: Indie Film Faces a Tougher Market — But Theatrical Breakouts Offer Hope 31 minutes ago How the American French Film Festival Is Bringing French Cinema to 3,000 Los Angeles High School Students With Packed Screenings of ‘In Waves’ 15 hours ago French Judo Legend Teddy Riner Announces 2027 Presidential Bid, Drawing Praise From Emmanuel Macron 15 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source River courtesy TIFF The indie film biz head into this year’s American Film Market amid one of the industry’s most tumultuous periods in recent memory. The completion of Paramount Skydance’s merger with Warner Bros. Discovery and Netflix’s leadership shake-up have triggered a wave of layoffs and cuts within the last month, while streamers across the board are becoming much more selective about acquisitions. For indie producers, sales agents and distributors, the upheaval means fewer buyers and projects, and an increasingly competitive marketplace. Yet the business has also been reshaped in ways that give reason for optimism. Theatrical is once again the engine of the indie economy, and Gen Z audiences are driving some of the year’s surprise hits, from “Obsession” to “Backrooms,” and, most recently, the nearly three-hour doc “You Can See Everything.” “We’re going to see so many more of these stories dominating in the box office. It’s what audiences want to see. If you look at the data and you look at what’s happening in the industry, the strongest, the best-positioned players in this sector are the independents,” says Jackie Brenneman, a former top executive at the National Assn. of Theatre Owners, who in January was appointed president and CEO of the Independent Film & Television Alliance, which organizes the American Film Market. Related Stories Olivia Rodrigo, Katseye and Sienna Spiro to Be Honored at Variety’s 10th Annual Hitmakers Event Raye to Headline BST Hyde Park With Sienna Spiro Opening AFM runs Nov. 10-15. Brenneman is preparing to oversee her first AFM with an expanded program aimed at attracting more filmmakers, financiers, exhibitors and technology companies to “show the broader industry why independent films are incredibly investable and why you should be bullish on independent film.” AFM also faces fresh competition from Toronto’s new market, but accreditation numbers for the L.A.-set event are on par with last year, with more than 80 countries represented among registered buyers. The U.S. leads, followed by Germany, the U.K., South Korea, Spain and France. China is also returning after several years of limited turnout. Heading into AFM, the mood among buyers and sellers is hopeful but cautious, with several predicting a busy market. “There are a lot of people crossing their fingers that it’s a strong market and there’s a lot of stuff there. I think the appetite is there for movies, especially after Toronto. The projects just need to be there,” says Scott Shooman, head of IFC Entertainment Group. Fabien Westerhoff, CEO of London-based European sales outfit Film Constellation, describes the current mood as a “dual, conflicting emotional state.” On one hand, he points to over-indexing specialty titles such as his company’s queer adult animation “Jim Queen,” which grossed $3 million at the French box office, and the doc feature “The History of Concrete,” which just passed $2.5 million in the U.S. Such hits, he says, have reinvigorated specialty distributors after years of “streaming hegemony.” On the other hand, Westerhoff says the “box office is extremely polarized around a handful of films, which isn’t healthy.” Domestic box office reached $8.28 billion from Jan. 1 through Oct. 28, up 20.8% from the same period in 2025, according to Box Office Mojo, but at the same time, fewer films are getting a real shot, as only 68 features had wide releases through summer 2026, down 14% from the same period in 2019, according to Rentrak. For David Atlan-Jackson, chief operating officer of European distribution group Vuelta, the business has narrowed to a single question: Does the film work in cinemas? “We’ve entered an increasingly binary, black-and-white market. Either a film gets a theatrical release or it essentially disappears. Television broadcasters have pulled back considerably, and everything now depends on theatrical success,” says the executive, whose banner is behind Bertrand Bonello’s next film “Santo Subito!,” starring Mark Ruffalo and Charlotte Rampling, which is in post-production and has yet to land a U.S. deal. “Every other revenue stream has become a multiplier of theatrical performance. If your film doesn’t succeed theatrically, you’re facing a real commercial failure. There’s very little middle ground anymore,” says Atlan-Jackson. A soft opening in theaters isn’t always fatal, though, points out Nick Shumaker, head of AC Independent, the sales and finance arm of Anonymous Content. “Look at the success of ‘The Apprentice’ on VOD: It got released, but it certainly didn’t solicit the theatrical numbers that I think some people would have really wanted it to, but it over-indexed on VOD in a huge way without ever finding a streaming home for obvious reasons,” he says. He hopes the same will be true for Alex Gibney’s “Musk,” which has struggled in theaters but is he says “is second only to ‘The Odyssey’ in VOD preorders on Apple. … We’re already seeing the Elon Musk film over-index on VOD pre-orders and it’s a four-hour film,” he says. Shooman agrees, pointing to three IFC releases this year, “Forbidden Fruits,” “Over Your Dead Body” and “Motor City,” which didn’t turn out to be box office hits but went on to perform well on VOD. The films that do break through are also proving harder to predict. A24’s “You Can See Everything” has become one of the year’s most improbable B.O. sensations, bolstered by social media buzz. It grossed $15.6 million during its opening weekend and has since climbed to more than $45 million domestically. Creator-driven films such as “Obsession” and “Backrooms” have also shown the appeal of projects built around online audiences. “What’s exciting is knowing success can come from anywhere: a found-footage horror, a politically socially relevant documentary, or a classic historical melodrama that moves you to tears,” says Westerhoff. Buyers, he says, “want films that can be eventized, generate word-of-mouth and fandom.” Shooman says the year’s surprises haven’t changed his thinking. “Does it make me rethink what’s a commercially viable film? No. I think the same holds true in that if you have a unique perspective, great access, a filmmaking talent, a story that people want to talk about, that still is, I think, at the core of moviegoing,” he says. “And when you look at the box office this year, three independent films had a bigger second weekend off of the semi-wide first weekend, being ‘Buddy,’ ‘You Can See Everything’ and ‘Obsession.’ So I think there is an appetite for audiences to come back. They want something that they can talk about.” The breakouts of “Backrooms” and “Obsession” have also sent buyers scrambling for the next creator-filmmaker. “I think everyone this summer suddenly said, ‘Oh, we have to scrub the internet for YouTubers because of ‘Backrooms’ and ‘Obsession.’ But the reality is the younger audience is a lot more welcoming to genre films, and YouTube is just where a new generation of filmmakers who have a phone and a laptop and can create content on their own are exhibiting their art,” says Shooman, who also notes that the biggest deals at major festivals consistently are genre films, citing “River,” “Leviticus,” “Talk to Me” and “Obsession.” Brenneman is looking to bring digital creators into the AFM fold with the launch of the Global Screen Economy Summit, which will feature a dedicated creator-economy discussion with executives from Spotter, Kynetic Media Ventures and Bamboo Bridge, along with creator entrepreneur Tyler Chou. “Some creator filmmakers are going to just be filmmakers, and some of them are going to want to become studios and sales agents. And those are the ones I need to ensure are part of IFTA. They are not a threat, they’re more people making and selling content across borders,” she says. “So anyone who is in that business belongs at AFM, belongs in our tent, and belongs on our stages.” Financing is getting more complicated and with pre-sales harder to come by, the money behind independent films is also changing. “Equity has stepped in,” says Westerhoff. He adds that equity brings “downward pressure” on budgets and more reliance on soft money to limit commercial exposure. “That’s why we structure our projects around European shoots, leveraging equity against international and U.S. rights.” Pre-sales remain essential above a certain budget, says Shumaker. “You just have to be really specific about the films and realistic about what the expectations are in terms of the necessity of presales to greenlight certain types of films. We’ve been happy on Mia Hansen-Løve’s new film [‘If Love Should Die’] in terms of the presales on that. So again, it really just depends on the film. If you’ve got a $50 million or $60 million action film, you need to pre-sell a whole bunch to greenlight that film.” In Europe, ambitious projects increasingly get financed through multi-territory co-productions, with the budget raised from several countries and production spending allocated accordingly. That’s the case with “Santo Subito!,” which is produced by Mandarin in France, with Vuelta co-producing in Italy, where much of the film is being shot. While the U.S. box office rebound is good news for international players, they’re lamenting the scarcity of buzzy American projects available for indie buyers and the growing difficulty of securing domestic distribution. If a film doesn’t get a U.S. theatrical release or ends up going directly to a streaming platform, “it becomes much harder for us to establish it in our territories,” says Atlan-Jackson. Shumaker points out it’s always been hard to find distribution in the U.S. “There’s a paradigmatic shift that has been happening for quite some time where a lot of distributors either want to be involved in third-party films earlier, or they are developing their own material. So as a result, they’re not buying as much at the completed film stage, with exceptions,” says Shumaker, citing Netflix’s acquisitions of “La Bola Negra” and “Gentle Monster,” which were unveiled at Cannes. Powerhouse indies, such as A24 and Neon, are in the position to not only acquire worldwide rights and but also handle international sales themselves. “I consider them studios. They’re not just producing their own films. They’re also acquiring films and controlling their international distribution, and when they resell the film internationally, they charge significantly more than the original sales agent would have,” says Atlan-Jackson. He uses “Club Kid,” Jordan Firstman’s Cannes breakout, as an example: A24 bought worldwide rights for $17 million from UTA and Charades at the festival after a bidding war. “‘Club Kid’ became much more expensive for independent distributors through A24 than it had been through Charades,” says Atlan-Jackson, noting that “they handle the marketing, the awards campaigns, the theatrical release — everything. They give the film real value. And naturally, they want to capitalize on the value they’ve created. That’s why they can resell a film for three, four or five times the original price.” Yet for international buyers balking at pricey U.S. packages, Shooman has a ready answer. “International buyers tend to complain all the time, and all it takes is them having pre-bought an ‘Obsession’ or a ‘River’ or a ‘Backrooms’ or a ‘You Can See Everything’ for that thing they felt like maybe they paid too much for to end up being a fantastic deal,” says Shooman. Alex Ritman contributed to this report. title: From a Mockbuster Version of ‘The Odyssey’ to a ‘Jiu-Jitsu Nun’: How Producers Are Keeping the Low-Budget Film Market Alive Via Streaming and FAST Channels (and Even Lower Budgets)
full_text: × Nov 10, 2026 8:15am PT From a Mockbuster Version of ‘The Odyssey’ to a ‘Jiu-Jitsu Nun’: How Producers Are Keeping the Low-Budget Film Market Alive Via Streaming and FAST Channels (and Even Lower Budgets) By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest From a Mockbuster Version of ‘The Odyssey’ to a ‘Jiu-Jitsu Nun’: How Producers Are Keeping the Low-Budget Film Market Alive Via Streaming and FAST Channels (and Even Lower Budgets) 31 minutes ago Kiah Roache-Turner Reunites With ‘Furiosa’ Star Alyla Browne on ‘Horrifically Creepy’ Road Movie Horror ‘Don’t Look’: ‘There Are Scenes That Are Going to Traumatize People’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Former Hello Sunshine and AGC Studios Execs Wifreddy Chiang and Anant Tamirisa Launch Baseline Media 24 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy The Asylum “Our journey begins with the Cyclops,” says a ginger-bearded and bald Odysseus somewhat nonchalantly in the trailer for “ The Odyssey ,” moments before a giant one-eyed AI-generated monster bursts onto the screens. The film, based — rather loosely — on Homer’s epic poem, released this summer and was met with mostly comic derision and a flurry of one-star reviews. “Dumb, ridiculous, embarrassing, nonsensical,” wrote one online critic. “Not a single redeeming feature,” bellowed another. But this “Odyssey” was not Christopher Nolan’s $250 million “Odyssey,” the epic from Universal, something many online said they’d discovered only after buying the film online. Nor was this the “historical accurate” retelling touted by Elon Musk and made using Grok. This was the $250,000 version from the Asylum , the B-movie icons and American Film Market stalwarts both loved and loathed for its vast number of so-called “mockbuster” rip-offs, its cult “Sharknado” franchise and an array of ludicrous film posters often involving multiple-headed monsters. In fairness, “The Odyssey” — thanks to being in the public domain for roughly 2,500 years — isn’t strictly a mockbuster. The title didn’t need to be tweaked for copyright reasons, like the Asylum did with other self-aware cash-ins “Top Gunner,” “The Da Vinci Treasure,” “Jurassic Domination,” “Alien Disclosure Day,” “Immortal Combat” and many more. But the film was absolutely made and timed to ride on the $125 million M&A coattails of Universal’s pic and, the company claims, succeeded. “It performed very well,” says David Rimawi, CEO and co-founder of the Asylum. “We’ve said this before, but we’ve found there’s a direct correlation between how well the studio film does and how well ours does. If it’s a hit, ours is generally a hit as well.” Related Stories Raye Wins Mercury Prize for Album of the Year Raye Named Variety’s 2026 Hitmaker of the Year “The Odyssey” Courtesy of The Asylum Other recent Asylum mockbuster hits include “The Last Hail M.A.R.Y.,” a sci-fi with a similar Earth-saving theme to Amazon MGM’s “Project Hail Mary” (but, instead of a CGI alien rock creature, it’s “a dude with some prosthetics,” says the Asylum co-founder David Latt); “The Mummy,” a totally different horror story to “Lee Cronin’s The Mummy” yet released around the same time; and, more recently, zombie copycat “Resident Dead.” (The company notes that it chose not to make a low-budget version of “Digger”). But success today is markedly different to how it was two decades ago. Back in 2005, the Asylum shocked itself by selling around 100,000 DVDs of its $500,000 “War of the Worlds,” its first — and, it claims, mostly coincidental — mockbuster, released just a day before Paramount’s Tom Cruise-led behemoth. In the years that followed, its DVDs — often cunningly designed to look like a major Hollywood release or with outlandish graphics that disguised the tiny budget — would line the shelves at Walmart, ready to lure in either the comically aware, cinematically curious, foolishly unsuspecting or just plain short-sighted. (The latter is something the Asylum tipped a meta and tongue-in-cheek hat at in its 25th anniversary title “2025 Armageddon,” featuring a scene in which a grandmother mistakenly buys one of its DVDs rather than a studio film.) But that highly-profitable physical market has long since come crashing down and, with it, the spoils. For its slate of mockbusters, monster thrillers and disaster movies, the Asylum now operates in what Rimawi describes as the “tiny margin world” of digital, mostly reliant on volume and the occasional breakout to lift the overall tide. “We actually have to make more to make a little,” notes Latt. There is still business to be made, however, with ad-based streaming platforms, such as Tubi, Roku and Pluto TV having come to the rescue in recent years. “This is where our customers and the Asylum found each other again, and if you’re watching the wrong movie, you can gloriously just jump to the next,” he says. “It’s the core of our business model now.” There’s also the ad-based FAST channel (the Asylum has its own), plus cable-based rental and purchasing transactions, although Rimawi says this business has largely shifted to Amazon, where “some films can do nothing, but some can be massive hits — that’s where our big performances come.” Curiously, the Asylum also still shifts around 10,000-20,000 DVDs a year at Walmart. “It’s baffling to us,” notes Rimawi. “I think people just use it like a rental store.” The Asylum may be keeping itself afloat in its own shark-infested waters, but lurking further into the independent film depths, for fellow makers of wild genre titles, the challenges of today’s world seem even greater. ITN Studios has spent years churning out scores of low-budget horror and action-thriller titles about clowns, dolls, dinosaurs, scarecrows, sharks and other classic baddies. This year it comes to AFM with a slate including the wonderfully named “Mary Magnum: Jiu-Jitsu Nun” (a thriller about a former military sharpshooter who breaks out of a convent to rescue her former lesbian lover). The film isn’t its first featuring a woman of the cloth. Its “Bad Nun” franchise launched in 2018 (the same year Corin Hardy’s supernatural horror “The Nun” stormed the box office). With the DVD market gone, ITN is also plying its trade across platforms like Amazon, Roku, Xumo, Pluto, Peacock, Tubi and YouTube, many of them with revenue share agreements. “But it’s definitely a lot harder now,” says ITN CEO Stuart Alson, who says operating as a volume business is the only way to survive. “If you’re trying to make it or break it on one film at a time, that’s what can be challenging. But if you have a slate of films and you’re constantly putting films out, some win, some lose.” Thanks to ITN’s impressive library of more than 1,000 titles (just a few years ago it was releasing almost 100 a year), many of its older films have long since broken even — meaning any new earnings, however minuscule, help to keep the lights on. Courtesy of ITN Studios But for others, due to a growing oversaturation in low-budget genre, both the opportunities to grab money-generating eyeballs and the budgets to make these films have been dramatically squeezed. About five years ago, Alson says he was financing films in the $30,000 and under range, but even this microbudget has now more than halved. “You’ve got people making movies for $5,000,” he says. Brit duo Scott Champer and Rhys Frake-Waterfield were among those making scores of cheap-as-chips horrors for ITN, but thanks to their slasher smash hit “Winnie-the-Pooh: Blood and Honey” (ITN’s biggest success to date), they are now focused on their own “Poohniverse” of murderous children’s characters (the third “Winnie” film is currently in post). But they assert that the low-budget genre arena where they once thrived is dying out. With films, and so many of them, now battling for attention on VOD platforms, the pair claim that where DVDs in the past could effectively fool people into thinking a movie is a higher-budget production, online you simply can’t hide. “Often the trailer appears instantly, and straight away you can tell,” says Chambers, adding that the immediate availability of online reviews and IMDb ratings also plays into it. “People are just becoming more savvy,” adds Frake-Waterfield. “If it looks too low budget, why would you invest $5 when you could rent, I don’t know, ‘John Wick’?” While many in the industry might turn their noses up at this schlocky corner of low-budget filmmaking, there’ll be little to celebrate were it to actually vanish. As Chambers and Frake-Waterfield note, it’s an area where emerging filmmakers can learn their craft, as they did. But there are also many who love it for what it is. For all the angry reactions to the Asylum’s “The Odyssey” knock-off, there were plenty rejoicing in the audacity of the film’s existence and its unashamedly cheap, so-bad-its-good quality. “I’ve never laughed so hard,” said one, cheering at a supposed Greek warship that was “nothing more than a little rowboat.” It’s too early to know the exact financials of the film — the figures from the various online platforms and the splits from the complex rent-sharing agreements can take months to come in. But with the $250 million blockbuster original having topped $1.6 billion at the box office, the Asylum is confident its version — coming in at a thousandth of the budget — can make at least more than $250,000 back. “We’re very happy with how it turned out,” says Latt. “So we’re now looking forward to Christopher Nolan’s ‘Iliad.’” ‘GTA 6’ Presales ‘Far in Excess’ of Expectations Ahead of Next Week’s Launch, Take-Two CEO Says Indian Paranormal Horror ‘Numinous’ Wraps, Fearfolks Takes First Look to AFM (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Heated Rivalry’ Final Episodes to Release in 4DX at Regal Theaters Kiah Roache-Turner Reunites With ‘Furiosa’ Star Alyla Browne on ‘Horrifically Creepy’ Road Movie Horror ‘Don’t Look’: ‘There Are Scenes That Are Going to Traumatize People’ (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Chasing Summer’ Director Josephine Decker Says That ‘Filmmaking Is Lonelier Than Ever,’ So It’s Time to Build a Community ‘De Gaulle,’ ‘La Gradiva’ and ‘Alice: Pioneer Of Cinema’ Among American French Film Fest Winners- Film News in Brief Loading comments...

title: Sofia Franklyn on ‘Call Her Daddy,’ Alex Cooper and Hopes for a Scripted Adaptation of Her Memoir: ‘I Spent the First Few Years Very Scared. Now I’m Good’
full_text: × Nov 10, 2026 8:11am PT Sofia Franklyn on ‘Call Her Daddy,’ Alex Cooper and Hopes for a Scripted Adaptation of Her Memoir: ‘I Spent the First Few Years Very Scared. Now I’m Good’ Franklyn's memoir "Daddy Issues" hits shelves Nov. 10. By Anna Tingley Plus Icon Anna Tingley Latest Sofia Franklyn on ‘Call Her Daddy,’ Alex Cooper and Hopes for a Scripted Adaptation of Her Memoir: ‘I Spent the First Few Years Very Scared. Now I’m Good’ 34 minutes ago Hollywood Is Obsessed With a Cheeky Slogan Tee 24 hours ago David Schwimmer Reunites With His Famous Red Sweater From ‘Friends’ in Nostalgic Quince Campaign 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source It’s a week before Sofia Franklyn ’s memoir, “Daddy Issues,” officially releases, and for the most part, her nerves have settled. “It depends on the day,” she says over Zoom from a hotel room in New York City, one of her two home bases. Franklyn, who splits her time between New York and Italy with her husband, is back in town for a packed month of press. “I would say 90% of the time I’m incredibly excited.” Related Stories Olivia Rodrigo, Katseye and Sienna Spiro to Be Honored at Variety’s 10th Annual Hitmakers Event Raye Named Variety’s 2026 Hitmaker of the Year But the road to telling her side of the explosive “ Call Her Daddy ” breakup with Alex Cooper has hardly been smooth. When Franklyn first announced the book in February, her agent received a phone call from Matt Kaplan, Cooper’s husband and business partner, allegedly screaming on the other end, as Franklyn recounts in the book’s foreword. Anticipating the backlash, Franklyn had already booked an island getaway to escape the noise. This time, though, she has no plans to disappear. “I don’t feel a need to,” she says. “I’m in such a different place than I was six years ago.” The 240-page memoir, which hits shelves Nov. 10, is split into three parts: her childhood and upbringing in Salt Lake City, Utah, with her single mom, who had her at 20 years old after a one-night stand; her post-college move to New York City, where she met and moved in with Cooper and launched the “Call Her Daddy” podcast; and, perhaps the meatiest section, her side of their dramatic breakup and the experience of watching the podcast she helped create become a multimillion-dollar media empire — without her. She now has the Unwell Network, a name she says she came up with herself for merch years earlier, blocked on social media. “I found myself sobbing at parts that I thought I was so completely healed over,” she says of revisiting these moments over the past year. Many of the details she shares in the book are already out there (that Cooper was being paid more without Franklyn knowing; that Cooper secretly met with Barstool Sports founder Dave Portnoy to negotiate a deal without Franklyn). But the memoir also reveals new details about the behind-the-scenes operations of “Call Her Daddy,” including the involvement of Cooper’s childhood friend Muji Fricke, who, according to Franklyn, was on the podcast’s payroll for a short time before Cooper fired him without warning. “She’s gonna fuck you,” Franklyn remembers Muji telling her. According to Franklyn, Muji was an integral part of the “Call Her Daddy” podcast, even feeding Cooper some of her most memorable bits, including the viral “Gluck Gluck 3000” joke. “I realize it’s one of several jokes – like saying her favorite porn star is Lisa Ann on an IG Q&A – Alex has made that could not have come from the mind of a white, blond college athlete,” Franklyn writes in the book. She continues: “Muji’s ideas become central to the show, and especially to Alex’s persona: an overtly sexual, clout-chasing WAG wannabe. Off-camera, Alex and I don’t even find a lot of Muji’s sexual humor funny. But we take his knowledge – the good, the bad and the ugly of sports and dudes – and put it on Alex, a dabbing hardo white girl in a push-up bra…Comedy gold.” His involvement was largely unknown until now. “This is how the show was put together,” Franklyn says, “and I don’t think people actually know.” As a childhood friend of Cooper’s, Muji also had firsthand knowledge of her personality before the fame. “Cooper doesn’t have friends,” Franklyn remembers him telling her. “I’ve watched it happen since high school.” He was also one of the few people Cooper confided in during the early stages of “Call Her Daddy” — and, according to Franklyn, warned her that even then, Cooper didn’t have her back. “Even at the beginning she would take the lines I wrote for you, or just cut all of yours,” he allegedly told Franklyn. She remembers clocking those early warnings but still feeling an inherent sense of trust. She couldn’t imagine that her best friend and roommate, with whom she spent nearly every waking hour, could be capable of that level of betrayal. “I clocked it, but I think my knee-jerk reaction was to just run over to Alex. I was so close with her that I thought, there’s a reason that he’s saying that, and she’s gonna explain it to me.” “But I did clock it,” she says. “And I did start to wonder about how she functions in her friendships.” By now, the general story of their breakup is largely known. It dates back to 2020 when Cooper and Franklyn, then two years into their wildly successful podcast, sought to renegotiate their three-year contract with Barstool Sports, which owned the show’s IP. Portnoy offered the co-hosts a deal that included $500,000 annual salaries, a larger cut of merchandise revenue and full ownership of the podcast’s IP after one more year at Barstool. Cooper wanted to accept; Franklyn did not, maintaining that the terms were still unfavorable. Cooper eventually went behind Franklyn’s back to negotiate a separate deal with Portnoy, returning to the podcast as its sole host in May 2020. Cooper went on to secure a reported $60 million Spotify deal in 2021, followed by a $125 million deal with SiriusXM in 2024, while Franklyn launched her own podcast, “Sofia With an F.” Unsurprisingly, this period felt like rock bottom for Franklyn. She turned to alcohol, drugs and nicotine, moved back in with her mom and experienced intense paranoia. “I get fucked up to remove myself from the vortex of pain, of betrayal, and loss,” she writes. At one point, she snaps when her mom takes out her phone, paranoid that even she might be secretly recording her to sell the footage online. With the power of Barstool behind Cooper, the public largely believed her side of the story and painted Franklyn as a villain. Over time, that narrative has shifted. “The audience is smarter now, they understand media a bit better,” Franklyn says, marveling that TikTok didn’t even exist when they first started “Call Her Daddy.” “Now they understand how things work.” It helped when, earlier this year, influencer Alix Earle had her own highly publicized falling-out with Cooper after parting ways with her Unwell Network in 2025. Earle, who launched her “Hot Mess” podcast under the network in 2023, later accused Cooper of being “manipulative and toxic,” claiming she received little production support and learned of her departure through the press. Cooper has disputed Earle’s account, with the feud drawing renewed scrutiny of her business dealings. “Alix and I have obviously shown each other public support,” Franklyn says. “There was, and I hope this doesn’t come out the wrong way, some validation in seeing that.” “I remember my mom and I were both kind of emotional about it because we had been put in this world where you didn’t know what was real and why that happened to me,” she continues. “And so to see it play out in a very different way, but in a very similar way…there was some validation in that. But I obviously felt terrible for Alix.” Others have confided in Franklyn about their own experiences with Cooper. But sparingly, she says. “People are very scared.” It’s a feeling she can empathize with. “I did spend the first few years very scared, and sometimes I will catch myself being a bit guarded or a bit paranoid, but it’s very rare,” she says. “Now I’m good. I’m back to normal, back to how I…” she trails off. “Even better than I was before “Call Her Daddy.'” While she’s ready to put this phase of her life behind her, she’s also not totally done telling her side of the story. She’s hoping for a scripted adaptation of her memoir sometime down the line. “Nothing’s confirmed,” she clarifies. “I’m just hoping to put that out in the universe.” She’s learned many lessons over the past six years. The biggest takeaway? “Some people you meet don’t turn out to be what you thought.” “But you can’t live your life keeping yourself protected,” she concludes. “If you’re doing that, you’re not living your life.” Julia Garner Says Madonna Biopic Status Changes ‘Every Hour,’ But She’d ‘Love for the Movie to Get Made’ Fantastic Fest Award Winner ‘Bloody Tennis,’ Starring Sandra Guldberg Kampp and Helena Zengel, Sells to Further Territories (EXCLUSIVE) Phil Rosenthal’s ‘Somebody Feeds Phil’ Flies to YouTube From Netflix, With Lift From United DC Studios’ New Boss Jeremy Latcham Has a ‘Guiding Light’ for Superhero Movies: Would My Grandma Like It? ‘You Have to Make Them for Everybody’ Nurse John Sets 2027 Tour (EXCLUSIVE) Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Designates the Troubadour as a Landmark Venue; Going Forward, L.A.
