title: Brandon Sklenar on ‘Iron Jane,’ Body Dysmorphia and His Rapid Hollywood Rise
full_text: × Skip to main content Brandon Sklenar Leo Jacob Brandon Sklenar is taking a moment to catch his breath. Over the past few years, the 36-year-old actor has watched his career explode with co-starring roles in Taylor Sheridan’s Paramount+ series 1923 , the much-discussed Blake Lively drama It Ends With Us , the South by Southwest sensation Drop and The Housemaid , Lionsgate’s $400 million-grossing erotic thriller starring Sydney Sweeney and Amanda Seyfried. And he has four more star vehicles expected next year — Paramount’s contemporary Western The Rescue , Warner Bros.’ special forces thriller F.A.S.T. , scripted by Sheridan; Ramin Bahrani’s romantic thriller Vegas: A Love Story , opposite Maika Monroe; and Lissette Feliciano’s female bodybuilding drama Iron Jane , co-starring Eiza González . Related Stories Movies Katelin Arizmendi on Bringing a New Perspective to Action With 'Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother' News David Walliams Revealed as Previously Unnamed Celebrity Alleged to Have "Preyed on Teenage Girls for Sex" “I’ve pretty much been going nonstop for the last few years, and only just very recently, in the last couple months, have I had a moment of stillness to take stock,” Sklenar says. “And now that I can stop and look around, I’m like, ‘What the fuck? This is crazy.’” He adds: “I mean, I can sort of see the linear progression of my career, but the opportunities that have been afforded to me in the last year or so have made me feel incredibly lucky.” Sklenar grew up in New Jersey, and his journey to Hollywood stardom is the stuff of vintage kid-makes-good stories — the sort of old-school outsider triumph that has grown increasingly rare in the era of nepo babies, influencers and YouTube crossovers. “I was with a girl at the time, and we just put all our shit in garbage bags and didn’t tell anybody,” he says of his move west right after high school. “And we just drove, literally in the middle of the night, like a Bruce Springsteen song. It’s so cliché, but it’s true. We just left.” A month or two after arriving in Los Angeles, Sklenar approached a stranger outside Mel’s Diner on Sunset Boulevard to bum a smoke. The man turned out to be a manager, who told him he “had a great look” and invited him to perform a scene from A Streetcar Named Desire, later helping him find an agent. Years of background work, acting classes, plays and small film roles followed before 1923 gave him his breakthrough as Spencer Dutton, the adventurer at the heart of Sheridan’s Yellowstone prequel. Before his next wave of projects reaches audiences, Sklenar now says he’s taking a moment to focus on his well-being (he just recently kicked smoking). “I’m trying to check in and just see where I’m at — mentally, physically and spiritually — so I’m ready for whatever the next chapter is,” he explains. “I want to try to strengthen my foundation a little before the next train leaves the station, because the last one went like a fucking rocket.” Iron Jane is among the projects Highland Film Group is presenting to buyers at this week’s American Film Market ahead of an expected festival launch next year. Written and directed by Lissette Feliciano ( Women Is Losers ), the film stars Eiza González ( Baby Driver, 3 Body Problem ) as Janie John, a woman who turns to competitive bodybuilding after a childhood marked by neglect. Under the guidance of a former champion played by Sklenar, she embarks on a punishing physical transformation, finding recognition and a sense of control even as her pursuit of perfection threatens to consume her. Sklenar is a first-time producer on the project through his recently launched Vista Lane Pictures banner. CAA Media Finance and WME Independent are handling U.S. rights. The Hollywood Reporter recently caught up with Sklenar by phone from Atlanta to discuss the creation of Iron Jane and why it’s an especially meaningful film for him. Where are you? I understand you were shooting something today. How’d it go? I’m in Atlanta right now. I’m doing additional photography for this movie, The Rescue , I have coming out next year. We’re adding some extra scenes to the movie. I had been off for a bit, doing home stuff and whatnot, and now I’m back on set, and I’ve got a fake mustache on and a wig — and it’s kind of tormenting me! It’s always so funny when you have to put on a fake mustache and have to try not to feel like an idiot. You know what I mean? I’ve never been in that situation, but I can certainly imagine. It just feels so ridiculous. (Laughs.) There’s something about wearing a fake mustache that makes you acutely aware of the fact that you’re wearing a fake mustache. OK, let’s talk about Iron Jane . I think there are no fake mustaches in that one. No fake mustaches. I understand this was a film you were trying to help get made for a long time. Can you take me back to the start of the project for you? So I met Lissette Feliciano a couple years ago at a festival party. Jay Glazer, my partner in my company, Vista Lane, had met her and he introduced us. He mentioned she had this really great script about a female bodybuilder, and he thought I would respond to it. So I met her and we just really got on. She came to Santa Barbara, where I live, and we chatted and got to know each other. And I read her script, and I thought it was a really special story. I just loved the texture and the point of view that she has. The story was really coming from a deep, personal, emotional place for her and I really thought it was something I wanted to see. So I was like, “If I can have any hand in helping this become a reality, then it would be crazy for me not to do that.” And then over the next couple years, I was fortunate enough to step in enough good puddles that I somehow got to the place where I was able to help someone get a movie made. I woke up one day and I was like, “Oh, apparently I am now in that position. So let’s make your movie.” Eiza coming on board was also a huge part of that. So it was a best-case scenario, really. Tell me a little more about the story and your character. You play a former bodybuilder, right? Iron Jane is an inspiring, classic underdog story in a sense, but it’s also very fantastic. It has a very hopeful spirit, and it’s very cinematic, colorful and vibrant — very much like the world of competitive female bodybuilding. There’s a sense of pageantry to the whole piece. There’s the glitter and the lights, and their bodies are just insane, but at the core, it’s a heartfelt story about a woman trying to take control of her life and better herself. I personally was drawn to it because I grew up in northern New Jersey working in an underground bodybuilding gym. When I was 15, I was cleaning the floors, and by 18, I was a trainer, training everybody and running the whole gym. There was an MMA gym upstairs, and I would just train MMA all day and then train other people. I started doing martial arts when I was really little, like six. So I was living in that bubble for years, and I understood this world very specifically. I’ve trained with Mr. Olympias and seen them pose — the diets, the steroids, everything. And there is an element of Iron Jane that really goes into body image and body dysmorphia, which is something that I just really feel needs to be talked about more, especially in this age of social media and fitness influencers. This is something I’ve struggled with, so we really wanted to translate that, and Lissette was really open to working with me on getting across [my character] Josh’s dysmorphia and what he goes through. Josh is a former bodybuilding champion. He was on that path a decade ago, and then he got injured. His body just couldn’t do it. He didn’t have the genetics. Now he trains people and coaches them to be champions and compete on that stage. He meets Jane and takes her under his wing, and he just really puts himself into her entire world — her burning desire to feel better about herself, physically and emotionally. So he trains her to take control of her body and become Iron Jane. Are you comfortable talking about your own experience with body dysmorphia? How do you cope with that? Yeah, for sure. It’s something I’ve had since I was a kid. I was a little kid — short, chunky. I swam in a T-shirt and got made fun of. Then I had a growth spurt and became really lanky, and I got made fun of for that. So I started training a lot and got obsessed with working out, like, “I’ll show them.” And then it became a kind of obsession, and it becomes a very weird thing, where you see yourself completely differently than pretty much anybody else does, and usually in not a good way. It’s very much an ongoing process. Therapy helps for sure. If you look at me now as a 36-year-old man, you’d never guess it, but I still very much feel like that 12-year-old chunky kid — that sense of nothing is ever good enough. You have to find a way to check your self-talk, because that’s really where it begins and ends — but it’s easier said than done. I imagine you and Eiza had to train quite a lot and put on muscle to prepare for the film? I trained in a very specific way for the film, but it wasn’t necessarily about bulking up. I put on a bunch of size for another film I had done earlier in the year. I’m starring in this film Taylor Sheridan wrote called F.A.S.T. for Warners. It’s coming out in May. I played a Delta Force operator, and I got massive. So I was still kind of working with that foundation. For Josh, I wanted it to feel real. He’s a guy who used to be really big, but he’s not broadcasting his body anymore. He’s just a fit guy now. So I didn’t want to overdo the preparation, because you can tell when actors do that. Where there’s a shot of their body, and it’s like, “This was my shirtless day,” and they’ve done the water-dehydration thing, and now they’re unnaturally cut. I wanted Josh to feel much more lived-in and natural. There is a scene where my body is fully on display, and I’m posing, and the camera’s panning up and down — and I was so nervous. I’ve been pretty much naked in a film before, but it’s a whole different thing to literally be posing and have the camera panning up and down your body, detailing everything. When I was shooting that scene, I was so uncomfortable. Dealing with my issues, it was very challenging to work through that. But at the same time, I was thinking about Eiza, because she had to do that the entire fucking film. Every scene is about her body on some level. So, I was like, “Goddamn, if I feel this way, I can’t imagine how she feels.” She trained for I don’t know how many months, but that woman put in serious fucking work. It’s really hard for women to put on that amount of muscle. My partner is a trainer and a nutritionist, and I know how difficult it is. You’ve got to eat so much. But Eiza trained her ass off, and she got in incredible shape for this film. I just have so much respect for her. As you mentioned earlier, you’ve started your own production banner, Vista Lane Pictures. What is the motivation and vision behind that? Well, when I first set out to be involved in film, I always wanted to produce and direct. So the idea that maybe I could help shape the projects I’m involved in was very appealing to me. I’ve been fortunate enough to work with some great producers, who I’ve been able to learn a lot from. The company is still in its infancy. We got this first-look deal from Lionsgate, which we’re incredibly grateful for. I’m just trying to soak up and learn as much as I can. I love acting more than anything in the world and I want to make interesting choices. I want to be involved in films that are purely about the spectacle and taking people on an exciting ride, and also I want to do films that aren’t purely commercial, where we tell a unique, universal story — and maybe I can even change my own life by playing a character that will help me understand how to be a better son, father or husband. Selfishly, I just want to play the widest range of characters I possibly can. So if I’ve hit a point in my career where maybe I can help myself do that by starting my own company, why wouldn’t I, right? THR

title: Vietnamese Musical Hit ‘A Little Dream Of Me’ Set For North American Release Through Reel Citrus
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz Asian World Film Festival Reveals Asian Vision & Focus On Sections ‘Somewhere In The South’ Takes Top Award At TCCF Pitching; ‘Reunion Dinner’ Scoops Three Prizes ‘The Hit List’ From ‘Gangs Of London’ Director Kim Hong-sun Boarded By Finecut For Sales View All November 10, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source A Little Dream Of Me 30 Pictures EXCLUSIVE: Reel Citrus has acquired North American rights to Vietnamese musical A Little Dream Of Me and is lining up a theatrical release on December 4. Directed by Chung Chí Công, the film features an 18-track original soundtrack from music producer Phạm Hải Âu and was shot in Vietnam , South Korea and New York. Kaycee, Trần Doãn Hoàng and Hữu Châu head the cast of the film about a pair of young dreamers who chase music from Hội An and Saigon to Busan and New York. Veteran actor Hữu Châu plays the hearing impaired father of the female protagonist, which has drawn praise in Vietnam for representation. Related Stories News Vietnam's Mockingbird Launches Horror Duo & Comedy Drama 'The Happiest Cell' At Busan's ACFM News Streaming & Local Film Propel Major Asian Markets To $15B Content Spend This Year - MPA Produced through Chung’s Saigon-based 30 Pictures , the film grossed around $2M (VND44BN) in Vietnam, making it the highest-grossing musical ever, in a market where the genre is rare, and the box office is dominated by horror and family drama. Watch on Deadline Opening on February 27, 2026, with around 400 screenings, the film benefitted from strong word-of-mouth and within three days was extended to more than 1,200 screenings. It held the number two spot at the box office through its opening week. With four days, the title and theme song were trending on TikTok, YouTube and through Google Search and were generating more than 11,500 social conversations. The theme song passed 13 million YouTube views and peaked at number two on the IFPI Official Vietnam Singles Chart. The film also became the first Vietnamese release to host sing-along screenings, with eight sold-out sessions drawing more than 1,500 fans. A live soundtrack concert, another first for a Vietnamese film, drew 700 people. “This is a different kind of Vietnamese film – it’s a full musical, it is joyful, and it is a story about family,” said Reel Citrus founder and executive director Brittany Tran. “Audiences in Vietnam made it a hit by sharing the songs and singing along in theaters. We want to bring that same experience to audiences here. The Vietnamese title [ Cảm Ơn Người Đã Thức Cùng Tôi ] means ‘thank you for staying up with me’, and December is the perfect time to say it with your family in a movie theater.” The film recently made its North American debut as the opening night film of Viet Film Fest in October. title: Katelin Arizmendi on Bringing a New Perspective to Action With ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All November 10, 2026 7:42am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother,' Katelin Arizmendi Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios/Theo Wargo In Bassam Tariq ’s Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother , cinematographer Katelin Arizmendi takes on the action genre for the first time, bringing a distinctive visual sensibility to a film that moves between crime thriller, family drama and spiritual meditation. At its center is Latif ( Mahershala Ali ), a devout Muslim and professional assassin whose world is upended by his wife’s death and the demands of caring for their three children, in particular the search for breast milk to feed his newborn daughter. The unusual setup gives Tariq and Arizmendi a new way, within the structure of an action film, to tell a story about masculinity, faith and fatherhood, as concerned with emotional vulnerability as it is with physical violence. Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother premiered in Toronto and was released in the U.S. via Amazon MGM Studios on Sept. 25. Related Stories News David Walliams Revealed as Previously Unnamed Celebrity Alleged to Have "Preyed on Teenage Girls for Sex" Movies 'Aroma' Takes a Sensory Trip Into Loneliness, Fantasy and Forbidden Desire (Exclusive Tallinn Trailer, Chat) Speaking with THR at the TorunCamerimage festival, Arizmendi discussed finding that visual language with Tariq, the practical challenges of shooting the film’s elaborate action sequences and the experience of being a woman cinematographer working in a still very male-dominated field. What was your first conversation with the director about the film? Was it about the visual design, or did you start with the story? It’s always about the story and the characters for every project. I like to at least talk about that first before I start bringing up ideas visually. I told him what I was drawn to in the script, which is that it’s a fresh take on a usually more masculine genre of action movies. It’s about something this man is striving for, which is breast milk, which has no material value to it. But I also had a really strong connection with his daughter, who I pointed out I wanted to share as much weight as him, because she’s sort of the one who always shines a mirror back on him. And then, obviously, there’s the spiritual side of this, his spiritual struggle with his faith. I’m not a Muslim, so I was asking a little bit of questions about his faith. It started to naturally progress into some visual ideas, and then I made a visual deck that I presented, and we went through that. So first conversations are always just about my connection to the project. From left: Adia as Fatiha, Mahershala Ali as Latif and Jahleel Kamara as Qadir in Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother . Jaclyn Martinez/Amazon Content Services When you started talking specifically about the visuals, what were the key points? Were there particular touchstones or references you were looking at? I tend to always choose projects where there’s much more of a first-person perspective. So we knew that this story needed to be told through Latif, and that would guide how we would frame things, where the camera would be, or even whether we’d be focused on the back of his head during a scene, even if someone’s talking to him out of focus. We knew this would be a very subjective film. But progressively, it also becomes more subjective through his daughter, Fatiha [Adia]. By the end, you feel like you’re more with her during this journey. I had never done an action movie before, so I had some ideas, and I knew what I didn’t want to do. I didn’t want to have two films: a film that felt very emotional and grounded in the visuals, and then suddenly you go to an action scene and it’s a different movie. I wanted to make sure those married visually and felt cohesive. But you still have to shoot action in a certain way because you have to cheat some of the punches and the impact of hits and things like that. It’s tricky because I could have done every scene in one shot, like Oldboy or something, and been happy with that. But we also needed to make these action scenes feel very different, so they don’t just end up with the same visual language, and they needed to get more and more elevated, so the end really feels more epic. Ali’s Latif (right) with John Cho as Pastor Hwan in Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother . Jaclyn Martinez/Amazon Content Services We came up with different adjectives to assign to each fight. The first one is really about brutality, precision and calmness. We need to see that he’s a skillful killer. That guided how the camera was locked off and on a long lens, so it felt a little more abstract. I didn’t want to give it all away right away. The second fight scene is the strip club, where he’s mostly thinking about his baby, Aziza. It’s Aziza, Aziza, Aziza. That fight is messy and it’s always moving. That helped guide the camera, which was constantly panning around the room, shooting through reflections on Steadicam, tracking with him. There’s a messiness to the camera work as well. The third fight is the fight in his home, so it’s in his sacred space. There’s an awareness of his family and his kids and his wife. He feels remorseful. By thinking of those things, we knew we should be in a wide shot here. When he kills this man, we’re taking in the entire room and we see his kids’ artwork on the wall and the presence of his family around. The last one was really about being a warrior, revenge and epic scale. We referenced samurai films a little more and wanted that to feel really epic. We tried to do as few shots as possible. We designed a couple of Steadicam shots, and then there’s also what we call the transcendental perspective. Before or after every action scene, there’s a massive high-angle, bird’s-eye shot. It alludes to this higher being that’s watching him and judging him for his actions. Latif and Qadir in Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother . Jaclyn Martinez/Amazon Content Services You’ll see that as he goes into the room where he’s going to have that final fight scene at the mansion. We stitched together the Steadicam shot and a crane shot that goes up overhead. We were also very aware of prayer times because there are very specific times when people pray, and I needed to be very honest about the lighting for that. Even though the apartment was on a stage, I couldn’t just decide that something would look a lot prettier with directional, low golden light coming in if it was really high noon. I had to be very honest about that. The film has the bones of a professional assassin revenge story, but the family and religious elements are quite different in tone. How did you approach those transitions visually? There’s a lot more intimacy and longer lenses in the family scenes, especially with the baby, and that was intentional. We wanted this real closeness with the family. But we also had to check ourselves every now and then because even within those scenes, we had to remember to let things breathe and pull out into wides. At first, we started finding the lenses that we loved, and we found that we were on a really tight shot with a long lens, 100 millimeter. We were like, “Well, the studio is going to say something if we don’t start pulling out into these wides.” For the fight sequences, by the end we ended up on a pretty wide lens for the Steadicam shots. But I tend to prefer shooting with every lens you have in your set and finding a purpose for it and marrying it together. I don’t really love it when you’re not playing enough or experimenting enough with different ways to move the camera or different lens choices. I kind of already work that way, being able to marry scenes shot with really wide lenses with other scenes shot very intimately. So that flow was kind of natural to me already. Ultimately, what grounds each scene, whether we’re shooting an action sequence or an emotional beat, is the emotion of the action sequences. As soon as we grounded it back to that, it felt much more like the same film. The fight scene in his house, for example, we shot over about two and a half days. It was extremely fast, and we didn’t have time to get a shot that I felt was very important: a moment of breath when he falls into his kid’s room. It’s a high-angle, slow-motion shot that pulls up, and you realize he’s just destroyed his sacred space. I fought for us to get that because if it’s just this fight sequence, you start to lose that emotional connection with the characters. Keeping things like that in made it feel more cohesive. Ali in Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother . Jaclyn Martinez/Amazon Content Services Can you give me a technical breakdown of what you shot on, in terms of cameras and lenses? We shot on Alexa 35 with Panavision Variel lenses and Primo zooms, with a little bit of LF (Large Format) sprinkled in for more scale and scope. I had an incredible colorist, Damien Vandercruyssen, who added film texture in post and made it look as close to film as possible. What was it like doing your first action film? Have you developed a taste for it? I shot second unit for Dune , so I had done action, but I wasn’t designing those sequences. My job on Dune was mostly to keep the visual language of the second unit cohesive with the first unit. But I loved it. I love a challenge, and I love trying different genres and different kinds of scripts. I would do it again as long as I felt that, at the core of the story, the script outside of the action was something I cared about. I’ve turned down action movies that just felt like there wasn’t anything there for me to resonate with. Do you have a personal favorite shot in the film? I guess it would be the shot that sort of breaks reality and goes underneath into water, when his daughter is praying for him and she brings him back to life. That shot was actually inspired by a video that our incredible production designer, Akeem McKenzie, sent me. It was of these kids who were shooting with a DSLR through water. We’d been discussing what this moment would look like visually because it needed a really epic moment. Basically, Bassam was like, “The rest of the film’s not going to work unless we can figure out something that’s so exciting for him coming back to life.” I saw this video, and then I had the idea to start on him and make it look like we’re moving through the ground, then coming up underneath him, and it’s water. There’s significance in Islam for water. It signifies mercy, so that made sense. I approached the art director, Shawn [D. Bronson] and asked him to come up with a rig that we could do practically because I felt we needed to see the space practically through the water. It would be very hard to do this on a blue screen, or it would feel different. It’s a platform, and the camera can get below with a Libra head and then end up shooting through the water. The VFX made it look like the platform was still the floor. Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios Women cinematographers are much more visible in the industry now, including among Oscar winners . But is gender still an issue in the industry? I would say it’s still a problem. I’ve faced a lot of misogyny, even on this movie. Even when you get the job, sometimes you have to really prove yourself. I was basically treated by somebody who needed someone to blame for us not being able to make the schedule, way before we even started shooting. It was like, “Oh, well, she normally takes two hours to get her first shot up,” because he had talked to other ADs I’d worked with. I was like: “You’re comparing it to a movie that was shot in the desert with animals, where it was the director’s first movie, and we were shooting on film.” It was just so obvious that he looked around a room full of men and said, “Oh, well, look at this young female DP, she doesn’t know what she’s doing.” I’ve had experiences where I don’t think about it at all, and it’s not like that. And then there are times when I’m reminded, “Oh yeah, I am a woman, and there is still misogyny out there and judgment.” But I’ve also come up in a time that’s much easier for women than it was even for DPs 10 years older than me, and I’m very grateful for that. In some ways, it’s probably helped my career more than been a hindrance. I’ve come up in a time when people are more excited about hiring a woman. I also realize that by not wanting to talk about the fact that I’m a woman, I’m not really helping anything. I’ve stopped doing that. I’ve accepted the fact that I’m in a proud place in my career, and I have a lot of eyes on me. If I just don’t talk about the fact that I’m a woman, then I’m not helping any of the women who are aspiring to be where I am. You need to see more women in these roles. You have to see that you can do it to be able to want to try to do it. Seeing that there are women shooting action movies may mean there will be more women who want to do it because they know it’s possible. And it doesn’t all have to look a certain way, either. You can bring a sensitivity to it. THR

title: Tilly Norwood Creator’s New Project? An AI Talking-Dog Movie With the Co-Director of ‘The Lion King’
full_text: × Skip to main content By Steven Zeitchik Plus Icon Steven Zeitchik Senior Editor, Technology and Politics View All November 10, 2026 7:15am Add us as a Google Preferred Source A still from 'Storm Dogs.' Particle 6 Tilly Norwood may have divided the town and broke the Internet, but the woman behind it says she thinks AI can be all love, too. So she’s making a talking-dog movie. Eline van der Velden, the Holland-born, London-dwelling producer of Tilly, has been developing Storm Dogs , a hybrid live-animated family film involving a motley crew of pups helping a toddler lost in the woods get home. And she’s hired The Lion King co-director Rob Minkoff to helm it. The film will use AI generations for the child and its wide range of canine breeds (with human voice actors) and adult actors for select live-action scenes. “I wanted to make a film that needed to be made with AI,” van der Velden, whose Particle 6 will produce the movie, tells The Hollywood Reporter . “Dogs are talking so that’s never really been possible [as convincingly] with normal animation or CGI before, and also you never want to shoot with dogs and toddlers. We’re using AI in a whole new way,” she adds. (You can see a teaser below.) Perhaps most notable for the project is the recruitment of Minkoff, the veteran family filmmaker (he also directed the first two Stuart Little films and in 2014 was behind the well-regarded DreamWorks Animation sci-fi adventure Mr. Peabody & Sherman) — and whose involvement can’t but be seen as a coup for the AI upstarts of van der Velden and Particle 6. “Eline pitched the idea to me and I thought ‘this is the best use-case of the technology,’” Minkoff tells THR, hastening to add that he is not involved in any way with nor does he endorse Tilly Norwood. “I’ve worked with animals and I’ve worked with children and I known how difficult it is. With animals in particular it borders on the inhuman to put them through the paces of a movie set. And now we can bring them to life in the way the story needs without any of that.” The film’s use of an AI generation for a two-year-old is also a good use case, Minkoff says; he used human toddlers for Stuart Little and found such an effort wanting at best and often downright unfair, both to crew and child. Getting the animals in Storm Dogs to move congruously and convincingly, Minkoff acknowledged, won’t be in easy. Dogs shot in close up have very specific features of the kind AI can struggle to match, particularly from one scene to the next. van der Velden and her team built the tool using existing models; the group is also using the veteran 3D animation software Blender to create their work. The Particle 6 team — it also includes tech guru Filip Parulski, who says a group of new tools will “help us actually direct rather than spend time in the ‘AI casino'” — aim to show the above 2 1/2 minute proof-of- concept at select public events and to players in the industry. Minkoff estimates that developing the story and creating the right generations as well as script-polishing, editing, shooting live footage and other tasks to complete the film should take about a year — not an overnight process but also not the eons-long effort that animated and hybrid movies often require. (He is pictured below right, working on the movie.) The film is being financed via a private donor who is behind Particle 6 and will be seeking studio distribution deeper into the process. Producers hope that Storm Dogs offers a kind of business disruption as well. Given their costs, animated family films tend to be financed and produced mainly by large studios.But AI can sufficiently reduce costs, van der Velden and Minkoff say, that it could allow for a new indie flowering in the space as well — only with technology instead of private equity and foreign pre-sales. Minkoff says that as much as the movie could serve as a proving ground for AI in family films, he doesn’t want audiences to notice or even know how he made it. “We are all the in the magic business; all of these tools are meant to serve an illusion,” he says. “If people are aware of the magician then they’re paying attention to the wrong thing.” Minkoff is touching on an issue that will only become more prevalent. Hollywood likes to hide the ball under the tophat. But it doesn’t want to be engaging in rampant deepfakes either, and how to use AI without making audiences feel like they’re being misled will be among the challenges filmmakers face as they roll out AI generations more widely. The 40-year animation and family-entertainment veteran says he does find parallels in this regard to CGI animation. “With that tech I thought the early tests were incredibly crude and a computer wasn’t going to revolutionize the animation business; people weren’t going to go for it. And now we see how that’s evolved,” he says. “I think we will see the same thing here.” van der Velden says she’d understand why some might be skeptical of what she’s doing with Storm Dogs given the auspices but feels the finished product will help overcome those reservations. “It’s a fun new way to tell a story that will hopefully bring a lot of joy to people,” she says. “This really is a wholesome family story that could not have been told this way before.” In general, she notes, “My husband says you can’t be doing pioneering work and expect everyone to love you, so you’ve just got to suck it up.” Meanwhile the Tilly train rattles on. van der Velden is producing the AI-generated sci-fi feature Misaligned with the character and rolled out the generation at a press tour in September to a fair amount of attention and nearly as much backlash. The appearance had some high-profile glitches, including an appearance on Piers Morgan’s show in which it spontaneously began speaking Chinese. But van der Velden says all of this is to be expected and furthers what she says is her true cause. “I definitely knew it was controversial when I started making her. But I also always knew my moral compass was in the right place and that she’s not here to replace any actors,” van der Velden says, continuing, “I wanted people to know before it’s here that this is happening, this is coming. I could have written a white paper but they weren’t going to listen to me if I’d done that. So I did it in a form that was a piece of art.” She added, “The result was what I wanted to achieve, which was awareness and people having the conversation. So the end point shows this was the right thing to do.” Rob Minkoff (r.) working on ‘Storm Dogs’ Particle 6 THR

title: Lisa’s ‘Always Lalisa’ Heads to YouTube Premium, Singer to Release New Single “Leave With Me” (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Nicole Fell Plus Icon Nicole Fell Associate Editor nicolemfell Follow Sign Up View All November 10, 2026 7:03am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Lalisa Manobal at the premiere of 'Always Lalisa' during the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Robin Marchant/Getty Images Always Lalisa , director Sue Kim’s behind-the-scenes look at global pop star Lisa , will soon be able to be viewed on YouTube Premium, The Hollywood Reporter has exclusively learned. The documentary, hailing from Sony Music Vision, premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival in September and made a limited-release stop in theaters last month. Lyor Cohen, head of global music at YouTube, told THR that the decision to bring the documentary to the platform was a no-brainer, given the platform’s global-forward focus. “YouTube has been such a big part of my journey from the beginning,” Lisa tells THR . The global superstar, a member of girl group Blackpink, speaks on the phone from rehearsals. Related Stories Music K-pop Star Wonho Announces 2027 Noche World Tour (Exclusive) Music Jisoo to Release Original Song for Upcoming 'The Angry Birds Movie 3' (Exclusive) “From sharing music videos, to my Coachella livestream it has helped me reach fans around the world so it felt right for me to share my documentary on YouTube,” she continues. The film heads to video platform on Nov. 18 and will be exclusive to premium members. The 29-year-old rapper and singer will also release a new single, “Leave With Me,” on Nov. 18. The song was made for and featured in the documentary. “I’m excited,” Lisa tells THR about people being able to watch the film at home. “Me and my mom went to theater to see the movie, but we were also like, ‘Oh, we can’t wait for this movie to come up on YouTube so we can just nonstop watching it.'” The singer says the reception to the documentary from people in her life has been great. Even some of her closest friends told her that the film helped them learn more about her, finding out about some of the struggles she’s had to overcome through the film as she had remained strong to those around her. Lisa recently released an EP Press Play in October, led by the pre-release single “SaWaDiKa.” In the time since that album dropped, the singer’s been busy preparing for her upcoming Las Vegas residency, which kicks off on Thursday (Nov. 12) at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace. The singer exudes excitement, and a little nervousness, about the accomplishment, as she’ll be the first K-pop star to hold a Las Vegas residency. “It’s going to be so much fun,” she says. “Everybody’s going to be there for me, [and] all my fans know every single of my songs, so it’s going to be a fun night.” The venue, which sits at just over a 4,000 cap, is intimate for the singer, who’s used to playing stadiums, arenas and festival crowds. “You can see everyone faces up close,” she says. “I know that they’re going to be so up close to me, so I hope that I can just [get] eye to eye with everyone.” THR

title: Skydance Bosses Throw Shade On Warner Bros Film Slate; Q4 Profit Will Take $200M Hit
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony Sundance Institute Names Allison Graff-Weisner As Chief Development Officer Saban Films Takes North America On Michael Madsen Action Thriller ‘Blood Behind Us’ – AFM Skydance Bosses Throw Shade On Warner Bros Film Slate; Q4 Profit Will Take $200M Hit View All November 9, 2026 3:53pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz Getty/Courtesy There’s a lot for Skydance co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz to be proud of in their purchase of Warner Bros . As Ellison said Monday during Skydance’s Q3 earnings call, “We have approximately $40 billion [in film] franchises which I think highly strengthen the overall portfolio,” and that “a new movie will arrive on our service every other week; film is a major driver of acquisition and engagement on our platforms.” Related Stories News Skydance Floats First Earnings Report As Hollywood Mega-Studio: Sizing Up The New Empire News Skydance Film Bosses Dana Goldberg & Josh Greenstein & The Warner Bros To-Do List: Pics That Are Ready, In The Works Or On Fire Despite potential plusses from the merger, Ellison and Kreiz also drew attention to the losses in store from Warner Bros’ 2026 film slate. More specifically, Ellison wasn’t shy in acknowledging that Paramount is in better financial waters going forward than Warner Bros on the feature side. Today’s earnings didn’t include the consolidated Warner Bros figures since the merger closed during Q4, just five weeks ago; still, Paramount brass painted a less-than-rosy picture of what’s around the corner. Watch on Deadline Said Ellison at the call’s onset, “The 2026 Paramount film slate is expected to generate $500 million more in lifetime profits than last year’s. We’ve now taken on another company with mixed results across the business…” He added, “We do have some headwinds particularly in studios where Warner Bros film has underperformed this year and will weigh on Q4 results. We’ll apply the same playbook we did at Paramount: greenlighting more selectively, prioritizing profitable streaming growth over subscriber count, optimizing linear and driving efficiency through the cost structure.” “We’ve proven it works, and we’re confident it will work again,” Ellison said, as the company is still looking at $6 billion synergies from the merger. Kreiz mentioned at the top of the call about the merger, “What I’ve seen, the various parts of the company are in strong shape. The Warner Bros. Discovery team did a good job managing their business and delivered the expected result through the close, with the one area of softness in the movie studio, and we are looking to build on their good work.” Skydance CFO Dennis Cinelli drilled down further on the red ink from Warner Bros, which saw right before the merger closed a major bomb in the Tom Cruise-starring political satire Digger , which cost $160M before global P&A and yielded $50.3M in worldwide box office. Cinelli said, “For the full year, Warner Bros is on track with our underwriting plan, with the exception of the near-term film slate. And Paramount remains on track for our 2026 guidance which is including the high-end of the profitability range at $3.9 billion adjusted EBIDTA.” The CFO added, “While the Paramount film slate continues to perform well, that will be more than offset by the continued underperfomance of the Warner Bros film slate. Based on this, we expect to have a $200M headwind to adjusted EBIDTA in Q4. That includes films already released quarter to date as well as films that we will release going forward.” The $200M headwind is essentially Digger , more or less. There was a report out there that Warner Bros’ 2026 slate was bound to lose $800M for the full year; we know from sources that is false. Even with the expected blockbuster success of Legendary’s upcoming Dune: Part Three , the WB slate is estimated to lose around $400M, per sources. It hasn’t been a great year at the box office for Warner Bros, with global box office misfires such as Supergirl, The Bride, Digger and no film grossing more than $100M domestic. However, the Burbank lot is slightly ahead of Paramount at the domestic box office year to date, from January 1-November 9: $569M (-70% vs. same frame in 2025) to $537M (+15% vs. ’25). Combined, the two studios count $1.1 billion at the domestic box office YTD, ranking behind Universal ($1.9B), Disney ($1.6B) and Sony ($1.4B). Paramount’s high points have been Scream 7 ($121.9M domestic) and Scary Movie ($108.2M). In a further sign to Wall Street that it is cutting fat, Skydance today announced the departures of prolific filmmakers James Gunn and Peter Safran as DC Studios’ heads . They are being replaced by early-2000s Marvel exec Jeremy Latcham, who departed the Disney-owned studio in 2017 before the explosion of Black Panther, Avengers: Infinity War and Avengers: Endgame. Ellison wasn’t all poo-poo on Warner Bros today. title: Kris Bowers On Creating A Love Letter To Ghana & Film History With His Score For ‘The Eyes Of Ghana’ – Sound & Screen Film
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Kris Bowers On Creating A Love Letter To Ghana & Film History With His Score For ‘The Eyes Of Ghana’ – Sound & Screen Film Dominic West Joins Irish-Set Drama ‘A Weekend In The Country’ — AFM Tom Rob Smith Writing Fiction Book Based On West Memphis Three Murder Case — Thessaloniki View All November 9, 2026 4:15pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source “We wanted this score to be a love letter to Ghana and to the history of film,” Kris Bowers says of his work on The Eyes of Ghana , the latest feature from Canadian filmmaker Ben Proudfoot. The Oscar-winning musician was speaking at Deadline’s Sound & Screen Film event, where a live orchestra performed parts of Bowers’ score. Related Stories Festivals Oscar-Winning Director Ben Proudfoot Talks Historical Significance Of ‘The Eyes Of Ghana’, Scoring Doc At Abbey Road Studios & Why Project Was A “Full Circle Moment” For Barack Obama Below The Line 2026-27 Awards Season Calendar: Oscars, Emmys, Grammys, Tonys, Guilds & More Directed by Proudfoot, with Barack and Michelle Obama and content creator IShowSpeed on board as producers, The Eyes of Ghana spotlights Chris Hesse, the 93-year-old forgotten personal cinematographer of revolutionary African leader Kwame Nkrumah. The Eyes of Ghana details the rise and fall of Nkrumah, a towering figure of African history who served as Ghana’s first President and led decolonial efforts across the continent. Nkrumah was toppled in 1966 by a CIA-orchestrated military coup. As a result, the films made during Nkrumah’s time were ordered to be burned. Hesse is the film’s unsung cinematic hero, along with his protégé, filmmaker and producer Anita Afonu. The documentary unveils a huge archive of surviving celluloid films from Africa’s liberation era in the 20th century, which were long thought to be destroyed but were quietly safeguarded by Hesse for more than 60 years. L-R: Dela Botri and Kris Bowers perform at Sound & Screen Film JC Olivera for Deadline Bowers and Proudfoot previously worked together on the 2023 short The Last Repair Shop , which won the Documentary Short Film Oscar in 2024. The musician said he became involved with The Eyes of Ghana after Proudfoot sent him a sizzle reel of the footage he was working with. “I remember watching it in my car,” Bowers says. “After I finished watching it, I was filled with emotion just because of how much, as a Black man, my own history is lost. And it’s sad that at some point you have to give up. So, the idea that someone like Chris Hesse has preserved this history and a vision of people that look like me that I had never seen from that era made me feel incredibly moved.” The Eyes of Ghana was produced by Breakwater Studios ’ Proudfoot and Nana Adwoa Frimpong, Afonu, Bwayo and Brandon Somerhalder alongside Higher Ground’s Ethan Lewis and Vinnie Malhotra. Barack and Michelle Obama are executive producers. The film was released as a one-night theatrical event across the U.S. and Canada on October 28. It is currently enjoying a sold-out run at DocHouse in London. The film also screened at the Dikan Center in Accra, Ghana. Check out the conversation with Bowers in the video above. title: 40th Australian International Documentary Conference Announces First Group Of Speakers: Poh Si Teng, Tamara Kotevska, Basil Tsiokos & More
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew 40th Australian International Documentary Conference Announces First Group Of Speakers: Poh Si Teng, Tamara Kotevska, Basil Tsiokos & More XTR Joins Oscar Contender ‘Y Vân: The Lost Sounds of Saigon,’ Award-Winning Documentary About “The Quincy Jones of Saigon” WETA And DC/DOX Partner On New $250,000 Fund To Support Documentary Filmmaking In DC Area View All November 9, 2026 4:43pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source AIDC The Australian International Documentary Conference ( AIDC ) will be welcoming some of the top talents in the documentary field to its upcoming 40 th edition. Among the first speakers to be announced: Poh Si Teng , director of Oscar contender American Doctor and founder of Tiny Boxer Films; Oscar-nominated filmmaker Tamara Kotevska ( The Tale of Silyan , Honeyland ); Basil Tsiokos , senior programmer, Sundance Film Festival; Rachel Antell, co-founder of the Archival Producers Alliance; Mandy Chang, CEO of Documentary Film Council, and Darren Dale, managing director and producer, Blackfella Films. Related Stories Podcast Doc Talk Podcast Goes Live With Director Poh Si Teng And Physicians Of 'American Doctor' Documentary 'American Doctor' Unveils Trailer, Sets Theatrical Release Date; Award-Winning Film Follows U.S. Physicians Who Treated Children Badly Wounded In Gaza AIDC, which describes itself as “the Southern Hemisphere’s premier industry event for documentary and factual storytelling,” will unfold from March 8-11 in Sydney – the first time the conference has been held in the capital of New South Wales in more than 30 years. An online marketplace follows, running from March 23-24. Watch on Deadline AIDC speakers. Clockwise from top left: Darren Dale, Poh Si Teng, Basil Tsiokos, Mandy Chang, Tamara Kotevska, and Rachel Antell. AIDC The conference also announced its theme for 2027: Reframed, which AIDC says “invites us to look at the same realities through different lenses: to ask who gets to frame the truth, and what happens when we challenge the narratives through which accepted points of view have been historically understood. “Through guest speakers and sessions, Reframed will call into question selective reframing through propaganda, misinformation, censorship and distorted realities, and will prompt us to harness alternate ways of seeing an existing truth through a contemporary lens by bringing in new, different and multiple viewpoints.” AIDC notes the 2027 edition of the conference offers the opportunity to “look back in order to look forward, acknowledging that our understanding of the world is never fixed and ever changing. Reframed asks us to reconsider what we think we know: to reveal what has been hidden, challenge what has been accepted, restore voices that have been silenced, and shine a light on what previous frames have left out.” In a statement, AIDC CEO and creative director Natasha Gadd said, “Celebrating our 40th anniversary as we embark on a new era, AIDC 2027 will be an essential gathering place for the documentary and factual sector to showcase not only what our diverse and creative storytelling community continues to create but to also actively reframe what the future could hold through bold thinking, innovative practice and radical solutions to complex sector challenges.” Gadd continued, “Through our 2027 theme, Reframed, AIDC provides a vital forum to explore and interrogate who gets to frame the truth, the forces that shape our understanding of reality, and to consider what becomes visible when we change the frame.” AIDC’s move to Sydney has been made possible by a new Principal Partnership with the government of New South Wales through Screen NSW. “Screen NSW is proud to support the return of AIDC to NSW for its landmark 40 th anniversary edition,” commented Screen NSW executive director Kylie Munnich. “With a packed line-up of compelling speakers and sessions, AIDC is set to bring together the best minds in documentary filmmaking, commissioning and financing from around the world. “We’re excited to see Sydney become a hub for discussion and collaboration, reinforcing NSW’s position as a leading destination for the screen industry. We’re also delighted to present the FACTory International Pitching Forum, which continues to connect talented creators with decision makers and to champion bold new documentary projects.” More than 750 Australian and international delegates attended AIDC’s 2026 edition. The organization announced a group of decision makers attending for the first time in 2027 along with companies new to AIDC’s market. title: ‘Being Heumann’ Composer Francesco Le Metre Tapped Into Judy Heumann’s Drive And A ’70s Punk Rock Spirit – Sound & Screen Film
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Matt Grobar Matt Grobar Senior Film Reporter More Stories By Matt ‘Being Heumann’ Composer Francesco Le Metre Tapped Into Judy Heumann’s Drive And A ’70s Punk Rock Spirit – Sound & Screen Film Alaskan Crime Procedural ‘Wild Life’ From Juliet Lashinsky-Revene In Development At NBC Untitled Signs Nnamdi Asomugha & His iAm21 Entertainment Banner View All November 9, 2026 4:45pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source For composer Francesco Le Metre , the brief when first discussing Apple Original Films ‘ disability rights drama Being Heumann with director Siân Heder was to capture the spirit of its subject, activist Judy Heumann, through music. With his score, he says, he was aiming for something “honest and intimate” — not “too big or too cinematic” — that reflected Heumann’s “personality, her drive, her humanity, but also at the same time, the impact that she had on the community.” Related Stories News Siân Heder & The ‘Being Heumann’ Crew On Creating An Inclusive Film & Production Environment – Contenders London Below The Line 2026-27 Awards Season Calendar: Oscars, Emmys, Grammys, Tonys, Guilds & More One throughline to the score was the sense of a “call to action” — the “big punk rock,” DIY spirit of the ’70s, which Le Metre captured through drums. “We had to deconstruct the drumming a little bit, so we played very unconventional grooves, and then also the strings,” he explained in conversation at Deadline’s Sound & Screen Film. “We performed the strings with a guitar pick instead of col legno to convey the sense of punk rock and, again, the DIY spirit of the movement.” Strings also helped, Le Metre said, to capture the sense of Heumann as someone with drive and racing thoughts who was moved to act fast. “I worked on a lot of string textures, kind of like these short phrases that were bouncing one to another. And I did the same thing with the melodic writing. When it came to her humanity as well, instead of writing a straight melodic line, I had small motifs interweaving into one another, to represent her thoughts or impulse.” Gaelynn Lea and Francesco Le Metre at Sound & Screen Film JC Olivera for Deadline Being Heumann marks the Sicilian composer’s first collaboration with Heder, the director behind another inclusive disability-themed crowd-pleaser in Apple’s groundbreaking Oscar winner CODA . Ruth Madeley stars as Heumann, who in 1977, led disabled activists in an occupation of San Francisco federal offices, refusing to leave until the government implemented landmark disability-rights protections. Others in the cast include Mark Ruffalo, Dylan O’Brien, Madeline Delp, Rob Delaney, Ray Fisher, Michael Patrick Thornton and Daniel Durant. Heder directed and co-wrote with Rebekah Taussig, adapting Heumann’s memoir. Producers include Heder, Kevin J. Walsh, David Permut, John W. Beach and Kevin Cleary. The film premiered at TIFF in September before being released in select theaters and on Apple TV this month. Watch the conversation with Le Mitre in the video above. full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg ‘Wanted’ Broadway Review: Historical Musical Plays With Gospel Truth UFC’s Dana White As White House Press Secretary? Trump Says “Please Take The Job!” Richard Lloyd Dies: Guitarist With Influential Punk Pioneers Television Was 75 View All June 16, 2026 5:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Paddington the Musical' Johan Persson Paddington The Musical , the seven-time Olivier Award-winning West End musical, is heading to Broadway : Previews begin Tuesday, March 30, 2027, at the Al Hirschfeld Theatre, with an official opening on Sunday, April 18. Based on the classic children’s book A Bear Called Paddington by Michael Bond and the award-winning film Paddington , the musical, by special arrangement with Studiocanal, features music and lyrics by Tom Fletcher, a book by Jessica Swale and direction by Luke Sheppard. Related Stories News Billy Crystal Sets Opening Date, Venue For Broadway Solo Show ‘860’ News Rosie O’Donnell Brings Solo Show ‘Common Knowledge’ To NYC This Summer The Broadway engagement was announced today by producers Sonia Friedman Productions, Studiocanal and Eliza Lumley Productions on behalf of Universal Music UK. Composer Tom Fletcher said in a statement, “It has been the greatest adventure of my career to be entrusted with bringing Paddington’s story to life on stage alongside my brilliant creative collaborators Jessica, Luke and our producers Sonia and Eliza. The response from West End audiences of all ages has been unlike anything I’ve ever experienced. It’s a great privilege to welcome New York audiences into Paddington’s world of curiosity and I am absolutely thrilled at the opportunity for this very rare and special bear to be on Broadway.” Watch on Deadline Casting for the Broadway production was not announced. “I couldn’t be more excited to bring Paddington to New York,” said book writer Swale. “As a city that breathes theatre, storytelling and imagination, Broadway is the perfect place to celebrate this exuberant and heart-filled story. I can’t wait. Let’s just hope Paddington loves Big Apples as much as he loves oranges.” Director Sheppard said, “ Paddington approaches life with curiosity, kindness and an unwavering sense of adventure, and what an adventure Broadway will be. It’s a dream come true to be bringing this joyful show to New York and I can’t wait for audiences to meet this very special bear that we all hold so close to our hearts.” Producers Friedman and Lumley said, “Producing Paddington The Musical with our extraordinary writing and creative team has been an immense privilege. Paddington Bear has endured for generations because he reminds us of the best of ourselves: kindness, curiosity, empathy and the belief that everyone deserves to belong. Wrapped inside a joyful theatrical adventure, with Tom Fletcher’s exceptional score at its heart, is a story about finding home, family and community in unexpected places. We have been genuinely blown away by the response to the production so far and are thrilled to be bringing it to Broadway. As the home of so many of the world’s great musicals, there is no more exciting place to produce new work than New York, and we cannot wait to share Paddington’s world with Broadway audiences.” The musical features musical supervision, orchestrations and arrangements by Matt Brind; choreography by Ellen Kane; scenic design by Tom Pye; costume design by Gabriella Slade; Paddington and puppet design by Tahra Zafar; lighting design by Neil Austin; sound design by Gareth Owen; video design and animation by Ash J Woodward; and hair, wig and makeup design by Campbell Young Associates. The West End production of Paddington won seven 2026 Olivier Awards, tying the record for the most the number of wins for any musical in Olivier Award history. The wins included Best New Musical, Best Director, Best Set Design, and Best Costume Design. James Hameed and Arti Shah shared the Best Actor in a Musical award; Best Actress in a Supporting Role in a Musical went to Victoria Hamilton-Barritt; and Best Actor in a Supporting Role in a Musical went to Tom Edden. The musical’s synopsis: “A small, lost bear from Peru arrives in London in search of a place to call home. A chance encounter with the Browns leads him into an unexpected world of adventure, where kindness has the power to change lives and strangers can become family. But London isn’t all afternoon tea and friendly faces – and even the seemingly happiest of families can have cracks beneath the surface. So, when a mysterious and vengeful villain sets her sights on Paddington, the Browns embark on a thrilling rescue mission, realizing they need this special bear as much as he needs them.” Bond’s A Bear Called Paddington was published in 1958, the first of 29 Paddington books he wrote, with the final one Paddington at St. Paul’s published posthumously in 2018. The books have sold over 35 million copies worldwide. Paddington has been adapted for television several times , first by the BBC in 1976 and most recently by Studiocanal, which developed and produced three series of The Adventures of Paddington with Heyday Films, Simon Quinn and Karen Davidson. Paddington has also been adapted as three big-screen outings developed and produced by Studiocanal with Heyday films and distributed by Studiocanal worldwide. A fourth feature film is in development with Armando Iannucci attached to the write the script with his co-writer Simon Blackwell. Also in development is a new animated Paddington feature film. title: ‘Here There Are Blueberries’ Broadway Review: Evil As Banal As A Bowl Of Fruit
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg ‘Purple Rain’ Musical: Jordan Fisher Is New Prince Of Broadway ‘Here There Are Blueberries’ Broadway Review: Evil As Banal As A Bowl Of Fruit ‘Wanted’ Broadway Review: Historical Musical Plays With Gospel Truth View All November 9, 2026 7:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Michelle Beck, Delia Cunningham, Kathleen Chalfant, 'Here There Are Blueberries' Matthew Murphy Here There Are Blueberries , the exceptional Pulitzer finalist docu-drama that opened Off Broadway two years ago to great admiration, finally makes its Broadway debut tonight at the Barrymore Theatre. The play, about a mysterious real-life cache of one-of-a-kind Auschwitz photos submitted to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum in 2007, remains as intriguing as ever – and with source material as grotesquely mesmerizing as these candid snapshots, how could it not? In fact, the sheer emotional heft of that photo album and everything it suggests dominates Blueberries to an extent that the play itself can seem rather thin at times, not entirely unworthy of the material at hand but not on equal footing either. Revelations about the banality of evil carry a force no matter how familiar we are with the concept, but familiar we are, and Blueberries can feel somewhat naive at times in its presumption that no one in the audience has ever heard of Hannah Arendt. But in the grand scheme of things, and in light of the historical tale being told here, those quibbles with dramaturgy shouldn’t diminish the real achievement that is Here There Are Blueberries . The play is vital and more often than not riveting. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News ‘Other Desert Cities’ Review: Julia Louis-Dreyfus Gets Seriously Funny For Broadway Debut News ‘860’ Broadway Review: Billy Crystal Remembers The Stuff Of Life And Loss Performed by an excellent cast – any production that features the great Kathleen Chalfant is an opportunity not to be missed – Here There Are Blueberries is, at its core, a detective tale. In 2007, a young Holocaust museum archivist named Rebecca Erbelding (Delia Cunningham) receives a letter at her D.C. office from a man who wants to donate a cache of WWII snapshots. Delia Cunningham, Kathleen Chalfant, Michael Cerveris Matthew Murphy The offer isn’t unusual – the museum serves as a repository for such keepsakes – but the nature of his collection most certainly is. The photo collection long in the man’s possession is more than a rarity, it’s absolutely unique: The images are of Nazi officers – including some of the highest ranking and most notorious, from Mengele to Höss – in their living quarters just over the wall from the camp’s atrocities. Some are of an almost surreal vacation lodge a few miles away, where officers, SS guards and female office workers alike would be treated to days of rest and relaxation for jobs well done. One officer is given five days there for his murder of two Jews attempting to escape the camp. Such images had never been observed in photographs before, and their discovery is nothing less than historic, generating headlines across the globe, with much of the public fascination falling on the young German female camp office workers enjoying their vacation lodge days and food-and-drink treats. “Here,” says the caption (in German) of one such photo, “there are blueberries.” The play is structured as an investigation, lead by the young archivist, as the museum staff seeks to uncover the circumstances under which these snapshots were taken, who took them, who is pictured, and, perhaps most intriguingly, how on earth did they survive when all over such evidence was destroyed by the Nazis themselves as the regime fell? One such question – how did the man who possesses the photos discover them? – is easily answered: A retired U.S. Army Lieutenant Colonel (Michael Cerveris) found the album in the abandoned apartment he briefly inhabited while stationed in Frankfort at the end of the war. Why he kept them in his possession, and did so secretly, is unknowable – he died shortly after making the museum donation. Other questions posed by the photos are of a more philosophical nature. Did those seemingly carefree young women at the lodge have any idea that the office work they were doing contributed to the genocide next door? And if so, how could they ? Conrad Ricamora (foreground, right) Matthew Murphy Blueberries , for all its demands on facing harsh truths, plays a bit coy in feigning shock at the answers, as if Judgment At Nuremberg never existed, an excusable but still noticeable manipulation. A bit more difficult to overlook are other red herrings seemingly designed to give the play momentum, such as will the museum board accept the donation of the Nazi photos when its mission is to chronicle the victims, not the victimizers? It’s a stick man argument. Blueberries is on sturdier dramatic ground when new characters – the relatives of the Nazis and camp workers in the photographs – begin arriving mid-show to offer their perspectives. The sister of an office worker sticks with the usual denials, but others are revelatory, not least the grandson of Rudolph Höss, who relates an unnerving tale of his family’s complicity and his own struggles with the violence he fears is an inheritance. The grandson’s tale is riveting, as is Brandon Flynn’s performance, a stand-out in a uniformly excellent cast that, in addition to those mention above, includes Conrad Ricamora, Scott Barrow, Michelle Beck and Montego Glover, all playing a variety of roles. Derek McLane’s stark set design, dominated by the many tall-legged stand-up desks used by the museum archivists to study the photos, is stellar, as are the crucial projections (designed by David Bengali) that allows us to see what the archivists are seeing. The photos projected onto the walls would be transfixing even without the superb lighting design (David Lander) and sound design (Bobby McElver) that further an entirely earned mood of dread and even despair, never more so than during a late scene that finally gives all those unseen victims their moment in this story, and in a manner so wrenching it won’t be spoiled here except to say that another photo album enters the story, and its story of survival is every bit as astonishing as the first. Brandon Flynn Matthew Murphy In the end, Here There Are Blueberries has sailed past its own here-and-there shortcomings to land on a final thought, artfully told and with clarity of conviction: Just imagine how many untold boxes of forgotten family memorabilia and grim relics are waiting to be discovered, with secrets as efficiently hidden as those sealed away in the human heart? In a new interview, Knightley opened up about fans approaching her and quoting the film, but it doesn’t mean much to her. “I have not watched Love Actually since the premiere, which was when I was 18,” Knightley said in an interview with Heart . “So, I think I’m the person that knows it the least of anybody.” She continued, “I know that people have a particular look on their face and then they say things to me and I know that means they’re quoting Love Actually, but I don’t really know what it is. It means nothing to me.” Watch on Deadline Related Stories Casting Breaking Baz: Keira Knightley, Stephen Dillane & Luke Thompson To Lead Stage Adaptation Of Oscar Winner 'The Lives Of Others' Into West End News Keira Knightley, Alicia Vikander & Jamie Dornan Set For Dark Comedy 'The Worst' -- EFM Love Actually is a Christmas romantic comedy directed by Richard Curtis and released in 2003, featuring separate love stories. Knightley played Juliet, a married woman who learns her husband’s best friend, Mark (Andrew Lincoln), has feelings for her. Mark professes his love for her with giant cards, while her husband is in the next room. Juliet gives Mark a quick kiss and returns to her husband at home. The scene is one of the most remembered, but for Knightley, it was only a week of filming when she was 17 and didn’t leave a lasting impact. In fact, in a 2024 interview with the Los Angeles Times , Knightley said one of the only lasting impressions she had of the scene was that it was “creepy” and “slightly stalkerish.” Watch Knightley’s interview in the video below. In a new interview, the Weapons star was asked if the film or series was still moving forward. “I don’t know,” Garner told CBS Sunday Morning , adding, “Every hour it changes, in a way.” The Madonna biopic was first announced in 2020. In January 2023, it was reported that Universal Pictures had scrapped the film . Madonna was set to direct the film about her life and career, penning the script with Diablo Cody and Erin Cressida Wilson. title: Jon Stewart Praises ‘60 Minutes’ & Ross Douthat For Donald Trump Interview: “I Think I’m Going To Enjoy This”

After gloating over all the Republican seats that flipped to Democrats, the Comedy Central host took time to react to Donald Trump’s 60 Minutes interview. Related Stories News Donald Trump’s ‘60 Minutes’ Interview Was A Mixture Of Denial, Reflection And Contradiction Following Midterm Drubbing News Trump Admits He Was “Only Kidding” About UFC’s Dana White Becoming White House Press Secretary On Sunday night, Trump sat down with Ross Douthat for an interview that left many pleasantly surprised. CBS has undergone many changes over the last year following Bari Weiss’ takeover, with many long-time journalists leaving amid allegations that they were being mandated to give Trump favorable coverage. Stewart aired a clip where Trump says his administration has “created wealth at a level that our country has never seen,” with Douthat adding, “including for yourself.” Watch on Deadline “Young man, was that sass?” Stewart said. “Did the new magnified CBS 60 Minutes just deliver sass to Donald Trump?” When Douthat pointed out that Trump’s personal wealth went up by $3 billion, Stewart said, “I think I’m going to enjoy this. I did not come into this interview thinking I’m going to enjoy this, but now, as I am watching this, I am thinking to myself, ‘I am going to enjoy this.'” Stewart also praised Douthat after he pointed out that Trump is a co-owner of a company with investors connected to the United Arab Emirates government. The 60 Minutes journalist noted that if he had told Trump that the Biden family had a similar situation, he would have called it corrupt. “I’ll have what he’s having,” Stewart said, nodding to Meg Ryan on When Harry Met Sally . Stewart continued to praise Douthat for continuing to press Trump, adding, “My God, Ross, you beautiful bearded bastard. Do you know what you’ve just done here? Do you have any idea what you just did here? You have made Donald Trump admit that the difference between him and Joe Biden is that Joe Biden is more aware of his surroundings.” The comedian also gave props to 60 Minutes for the timing of their commercial breaks during pivotal moments of the interview “for maximum dramatic impact.” Trump was asked if he would forgive any of his enemies in order to go to Heaven, to which he said, “Can I be honest? I probably cannot do that now because I do hate some of my enemies, and I always will.” The iconic 60 Minutes tick-tock then starts playing, with Stewart adding, “Oh shit! No, they didn’t. Oh shit! That is some Ebenezer Scrooge bullshit on that.” Stewart continued, “ 60 Minutes directed by [Ingmar] Bergman, now? Is there a sound that is any more of an ominous portent of the fate that awaits Donald Trump?” Watch Jon Stewart’s talk about the midterms and Trump on The Daily Show below.
